edits.chapter_key: abd manaf and the breaker of bread
edits.body_md:
'Abd Manaf was the finest of them, for Allah had singled him out to be the forefather of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family. It is said: "If a stone were found inscribed with the words, I am the jealousy of the son of Qusay — commanded to be pious — in the hadith, may God bless you." Indeed, he only commanded the fear of Allah — the Almighty — to be feared by those who truly feared Him and believed in Him. And this is among the proofs of the great station and noble standing of the Prophet's fathers, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.

Ibn al-Zuba'ari said of 'Abd Manaf:

> *A pure sign for 'Abd Manaf —*
> *the Quraysh were white and she was split.*
> *And those who say: Come to the guests —*
> *the feathers and not the feathers.*
> *They embraced you from Hawa and from Iqraf.*
> *Your mother was violated if you went to their house.*

Al-Khuza'i said:

> *O nomad who has turned aside — journey now, you are in the family of 'Abd Manaf.*
> *And those who departed for the Ilaf journey —*
> *those who took the covenant across its horizons,*
> *the journey of desire and the journey of summers —*
> *both journeys were enacted for him.*

Among them is what was said of Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf, who was called 'Amr:

> *And the men of Mecca are lean —*
> *'Amr, who broke the Tharid for his people.*

The Banu 'Abd Manaf are called "al-Tayyibun," because the presidency rested with them, and they sought to take the brigade and the veil from Banu 'Abd al-Dar. Banu 'Abd al-Dar formed a pact with other clans to prevent Banu 'Abd Manaf from taking what had been theirs.

Umm Hakim, daughter of 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, took a handful of perfume and put her hand into the stone, then said: "Whoever has been kind to him is one of us." Thereupon Banu 'Abd Manaf, Banu Asad, Banu Zuhra, Banu Taym, and Banu al-Harith joined together; they were called "al-Mutayyabun." When Banu Sahm saw this, they slaughtered a camel and plunged their hands into its blood, saying: "Whoever licks its blood is one of us." Those who did so were Banu Sahm, Banu 'Adi, Banu 'Abd al-Dar, Banu Jumah, and Banu Makhzum; they were called "al-Ahlaf." Then nothing further passed between them.

On this al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas said:

> *And we called the good ones from the Quraysh —*
> *What good had we ever failed to do?*
> *On the vineyard of Falat, Banna, and Taba,*
> *We never closed a door upon the people.*

Concerning 'Abd Manaf, the poet says:

> *More honorable than 'Abd Manaf in lineage —*
> *No mother bore a child of finer stock.*

Qusay gave 'Abd Manaf the watering rights, the rifada, and the house of the council. Qusay took the council house and set its door facing the Ka'bah, then divided Makkah into four quarters among the Quraysh. Qusay was called "the Gatherer," for — as the poet says — Allah gathered the tribes through him:

> *Your father Qusay was called the Gatherer —*
> *Through him, God assembled the clans of Fahr.*

Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im ibn 'Adi ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf said: "Qusay ibn Kilab was the first to reign as a king among the sons of Ka'b ibn Lu'ay." With all his glory, that distinction passed to 'Abd Manaf ibn Qusay and became his. Allah bestows His bounty upon whom He wills, and He placed the seed of prophethood in Qusay's line and caused it to take root through his heirs.

The honor of 'Abd Manaf then passed, by Allah's grace, to his son Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf. Hashim's given name was 'Amr, and he was called "'Amr al-'Ali" on account of his high standing. He was named Hashim because he was the first to break bread, crumble it into broth, and feed it to the people — and so he was called Hashim, "the Breaker." Allah honored him and gave him distinction through his closeness to the Prophet ﷺ and his family — the best of all Arabs and non-Arabs, the master of the sons of Adam.

It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ and the Imams of his household commanded Bilal ibn Hamamah to call the noon prayer one day before its time, during the month of Rajab, thirteen nights into it. Bilal did so, and the people stirred, saying, "Something has happened." They gathered in the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came walking toward the mosque until he reached Bab al-Shamiyyin — one of the mosque's gates — where he took hold of both sides of the gate. The mosque contained a place called al-Saddah. He then called out: "Do you hear, O people of al-Saddah?" They answered, "We hear and we obey, O Messenger of Allah." He said, "Do you wish to know?" So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"Allah the Almighty created the creation and divided it into two parts, and I was placed in the better of the two parts. This is what He said:

> ﴿وَأَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ﴾
> "The Companions of the Right Hand — how excellent are the Companions of the Right Hand." (al-Waqi'ah: 27)

I am of the people of the right, and I am the best among the people of the right hand. Then He divided those two parts into three, and I was placed among the best of them. This is what He said:

> ﴿فَأَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ ۝ وَأَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ ۝ وَالسَّابِقُونَ السَّابِقُونَ﴾
> "So the Companions of the Right Hand — how excellent are the Companions of the Right Hand; and the Companions of the Left Hand — how wretched are the Companions of the Left Hand; and the Foremost, the Foremost." (al-Waqi'ah: 8–10)

I am of the foremost, and I am the best of the foremost. Then He divided the third into tribes, and I was placed among the best of them. This is what He said:

> ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَاكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَاكُمْ شُعُوبًا وَقَبَائِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوا﴾
> "O mankind, indeed We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another." (al-Hujurat: 13)

My tribe is the best of all tribes. I hold them in awe before Allah the Almighty, and I am the master of the sons of Adam, and I say this without pride. Then He divided the tribes into clans, and He placed me in the best of them. This is what He said:

> ﴿إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُذْهِبَ عَنكُمُ الرِّجْسَ أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ وَيُطَهِّرَكُمْ تَطْهِيرًا﴾
> "Indeed, Allah intends only to remove from you the impurity, O people of the House, and to purify you with a thorough purification." (al-Ahzab: 33)

Allah then singled out three from my household for distinction, and I am the master of all three, and I hold them in awe before Allah — without pride. He chose me above 'Ali, Hamza, and Ja'far. We were once resting in al-Abtah, and every one of us had drawn his garment over his face: 'Ali to my right, Ja'far to my left, and Hamza at my feet. What roused me from my sleep was the rustling of angels' wings and a coolness upon my chest from 'Ali's arm. I looked around, and I found Jibril standing before three angels. One of them asked: 'O Jibril, to which of these four have you been sent?' He nudged me with his foot and said, 'To this one.' The angel asked, 'And who is this?' He replied, 'This is Muhammad, the master of the messengers.' Then he gestured toward 'Ali and said, 'This is the master of the guardians.' He gestured toward Hamza and said, 'This is the master of the martyrs.' He gestured toward Ja'far and said, 'This one — in Paradise he has a door with two wings, two gilded wings with which he flies.'"

This is evidence of the virtue of the Prophet's fathers ﷺ — and in particular of those nearest to him among them. This hadith is mentioned in the account of his grandfather Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf because it is through his lineage that the best of all households descends — and this is an undeniable virtue, established on sound authority.

We now return to the account of Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf. Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf held the guardianship of his father's rights in the watering and the rifada, and he held the presidency in Makkah above all his father's other sons. On the first of Dhu al-Hijjah, he would address the Quraysh with his back to the door of the Ka'bah, commanding them to do good and exhorting them to noble character. In his sermon he would say:

"O gathering of Quraysh, you are the masters of the Arabs, the finest of them in face and the greatest of them in forbearance. You are the heartland of the Arabs in lineage and the closest to them in bonds of kinship. O gathering of Quraysh, you are the neighbors of the House of Allah the Almighty — may Allah honor you with its guardianship and single you out from among the sons of Ishmael for nearness to it, and may He preserve in you the best that any neighbor has preserved. Honor the guests of Allah and the visitors of His House, for they come to you travel-worn and dusty from every land. As for my wealth, if all of it were sufficient for you I would give it freely — but I am a steward of my wealth, lawfully directing it, so long as no kinship tie is severed, nothing is taken unjustly, and nothing forbidden is mixed into it. And whoever among you wishes to give from his own wealth what he is able to give — I ask you by the sanctity of this House that none of you hold back from providing for the dignity and sustenance of the House's visitors, so long as what is given has not been taken unjustly and no kinship tie has been severed in acquiring it."

The Banu Ka'b ibn Lu'ay responded earnestly to this call and spent freely of their wealth. Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf would collect these contributions and store them in the Dar al-Nadwa until the pilgrims arrived, and then he would feed them. He would bring large waterskins from the vicinity of Zamzam, fill them with water, and set them out for the pilgrims to drink. He fed them in Makkah before the day of watering, and on the day of watering he fed them in Mina, at 'Arafah, and at the gathering-place — bread was distributed to them — along with meat, clarified butter, sawiq, and dates. He watered them with milk and crumbled bread for them; it is for this that he was named Hashim. He was also called "the Moon" in honor of his noble bearing and beauty.

In this regard, Matrud al-Khuza'i says:

> *The men of Makkah were gaunt and lean*
> *Until 'Amr broke bread for his people.*

He was the first to make the roads of Makkah safe. The Quraysh were a mercantile people, yet their trade had not extended beyond Makkah — until Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf rode to the Levant, where he came before Caesar. Each day he slaughtered a sheep, prepared food, and invited those around him to eat, for he was among the finest of people in character and appearance. Word of his generosity and fine bearing reached Caesar, who summoned him, honored him with special distinction, and showed him great favor.

Hashim said to him: "O king, my people are the merchants of the Arabs. If you see fit to write them a letter of safe passage, they will bring you the finest goods from across the Hijaz." Caesar agreed and wrote him a letter guaranteeing their safety. Hashim then took that letter, and whenever he passed through the territories of Arab tribes on the road to the Levant, he would halt them on the grounds that the Quraysh were carrying goods for them; he would arrange for those goods to be delivered, and he would return the tribes' capital along with their profit.

Hashim thus secured the compact of Ilaf for all those between him and the Levant. He returned to Makkah bringing with him more blessings than his people had ever known, and they set out with a great caravan. Hashim led them, and they continued to benefit from the arrangements of Ilaf until they reached the Levant. He died on that journey, in Gaza, in the land of the Levant.

In this regard, Matrud al-Khuza'i said:

> *A grave in Gaza holds Hashim — he does not pass away;*
> *The generous one died in Damascus on the day of his mourning.*
> *His absence is a loss to all who dwell in his yard;*
> *Hold firm to his memory, with tongue and with hand.*

Among the traditions that speak to 'Abd al-Muttalib's virtue, honour, and unshakeable trust in his Lord is the following account, concerning the Abyssinian campaign against Yemen. Abraha al-Ashram, the Abyssinian viceroy of Yemen, marched with the intent of destroying the Sacred House of God, bringing with him an elephant named Yaksom.

A Yemeni nobleman named Dhu Nafr rose against him, calling his people and whatever Arabs answered his appeal to wage jihad in defence of the Sacred House. He was one of Yemen's great lords and kings. He engaged Abraha in battle, but Abraha defeated him and his companions, took Dhu Nafr captive, and marched on with him in his train.

Abraha then confronted Nafil ibn Habib al-Khath'ami at the pass of Khath'am, along with two tribes. He routed them and captured Nafil. When Abraha intended to kill him, Nafil said: "Do not kill me — spare me and I will guide you wherever you wish." So Abraha kept him as a guide and marched on.

As Abraha's armies drew near the Haram and approached Mecca, the Quraysh realised they had no means to resist him by force. They withdrew, while 'Abd al-Muttalib stood firm and declared: "By Allah, I shall not abandon the Haram. I seek no glory elsewhere." He remained in the city while the Quraysh dispersed.

'Abd al-Muttalib said:

> *No, let them not think the Ra Yum concerns us —*
> *we shall settle it, so guard what is lawful to you.*
> *Though their prayers beat down and their encampments become your sanctuaries,*
> *do not let them overpower your Qurhan.*

The word rendered "impossible" here is al-Qurrah, as in the Almighty's saying, ﴿ مُسْتَقَرٌّ ﴾ [al-Ra'd: 13].

The Quraysh then departed, and 'Abd al-Muttalib rose greatly in their esteem when they witnessed how firmly he forbade himself to Allah and placed his complete trust in Him — a mark of his sound and penetrating judgment in divine affairs.

When the army of the Elephant drew near the outskirts of Mecca, they struck 'Abd al-Muttalib's camels and drove them off. Word of this reached Abraha, along with news of 'Abd al-Muttalib's standing and his position among his people. Abraha sent for him, and when he came, Abraha marvelled at his bearing, his dignity, and his commanding presence. He honoured him, seated him beside himself, and asked whether he had a need to present. 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "Your army has seized my camels — I ask that you return them to me." Abraha was astonished and said: "You have diminished yourself in my eyes and lowered your standing with me. You come to ask about your camels, yet you say nothing of this House that I have come to demolish — does it mean nothing to you?" 'Abd al-Muttalib replied: "Those camels are mine, and I am their owner. As for the House, it has a Lord who will protect it from you if He wills."

This reply made 'Abd al-Muttalib only greater in Abraha's eyes, and his words carried enormous weight with him. Abraha ordered the camels returned.

Then Allah vindicated the words of 'Abd al-Muttalib:

> ﴿ وَأَرْسَلَ عَلَيْهِمْ طَيْرًا أَبَابِيلَ ﴾ ﴿ تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ مِّن سِجِّيلٍ ﴾
> "And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of baked clay." (al-Fil: 3–4)

It was said that these birds resembled swallows or martins; each bird carried three stones — one in its beak and one in each claw — roughly the size of chickpeas or lentils. Any man struck by one of them perished, though not all were struck. The army broke and fled, scattering along the road back to Yemen.

When Nafil witnessed the divine wrath descending upon them, he cried out:

> *Where is the refuge for one whom God pursues? The victorious has no escape.*

Nafil also said:

> *We greet you with the morning — eyes that saw*
> *what your wing-tips spared us.*
> *I have with me a hedgehog we never saw before;*
> *grieve not for what has befallen us.*
> *Stones were cast upon us*
> *as though the Abyssinians had become our creed —*
> *did you love us? We gave no answer.*
> *We shall dine with you.*
> *Rudeina, if you see or find abundance,*
> *then excuse me and praise my conduct.*
> *I thanked God when I saw the bird,*
> *while all the people ask about the gheeel.*

The army fled, falling in every direction, perishing along every road. Abraha himself was struck in his body; they carried him away as his limbs fell from him piece by piece, each inch dropping away and leaving behind a trail of pus, until they finally brought him into San'a' in a state like a fledgling chick. He did not die until his chest split open.

'Abd al-Muttalib said concerning these events:

> *His heart, as they claim, was in what it harboured.*
> *His building demolishes the lyric —*
> *his fathers rushed toward the House of God,*
> *guided through the age of sin.*
> *You are firm, yet your wealth is not firm;*
> *you change grey hair after youth —*
> *so what do you wear as your alleged garment?*
> *Let your remembrance of the matter of union be forbidden;*
> *you are the one I dream of recalling —*
> *an army that came to you in al-Ashram,*
> *as though they were a people laden with spoils.*
> *The next day they were left like al-Battah,*
> *overwhelmed by what afflicted them.*
> *An elephant they led to the lowest ground —*
> *its Creator honours His close friend.*
> *Where is he who stood in his era?*
> *Their eyes were not shielded from the elephant.*
> *God repented of its destruction —*
> *as though its fountains overflowed with remorse.*
> *The Ababeel birds flew to pelt them;*
> *the stones lodged fast in Hama.*
> *He honoured the people of the sanctuary as the books record,*
> *and despite Abraha's arrogance he was compelled.*
> *With victory from God, the Lord of all servants —*
> *a promise rhyming true with right —*
> *the eagles became the scavengers of their remains,*
> *circling as mourners do.*
> *A land whose Zamzam was dug,*
> *and may God bequeath us the finest of lands.*

'Abd al-Muttalib also has these verses on the same subject:

> *We are the family of God in His town, as it has ever been since the age of Abraham.*
> *Whoever seeks to corrupt it will be silenced.*
> *The House has a God who defends it;*
> *even in the ancient days, it was cast into strife — and was preserved.*
> *I have watched the wicked dragged to their ruin.*

There was indeed a clear sign and a lasting lesson in the destruction of the Companions of the Elephant, through which Allah protected His Sacred House and forbade its violation. He manifested the virtue of its guardian and vindicated His prophet 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim — confirming his promise to him and answering his words: "The House has a Lord who protects it." And He answered his supplication.

That same year — the Year of the Elephant — saw the birth of al-Mustafa Muhammad, master of all humanity and seal of the prophets, may God bless him and grant him and his family peace. This was among the blessings heralding his birth, and his religion — peace and blessings be upon him — was thereby blessed.

Then 'Abd al-Muttalib received a vision in his sleep in which he was commanded: "Dig Zamzam — the hidden place of the Grand Sheikh." He awoke and said, "O Allah, make it plain to me." He returned to sleep, and the vision came again, saying: "Dig the troubled woman — none shall be able to withhold her from the people but you." Again he said, "O Allah, make it plain to me," and returned to sleep. The vision came a third time, saying: "Dig Zamzam, between al-Farth and the blood, where the crow alights, hottest above the village of the ants, toward the red monuments."

He rose and went to the Sacred Mosque, where he sat and waited for the sign he had been shown.

A group of people then slaughtered a cow, and it broke free from its tether and bolted into the Sacred Mosque, falling in the very spot of Zamzam. The tether was recognised, and its owner made for that place, slaughtered the cow there, and skinned it. A crow then came and settled until it landed in the manure, where 'Abd al-Muttalib found an anthill. He rose and began digging there for Zamzam.

The Quraysh came to him and said: "O 'Abd al-Muttalib, what do you think you are doing — digging in our mosque without our knowledge?" He replied: "I have been commanded to do this, and He who commanded me will repel anyone who tries to stop me." They left off when they understood that a divine charge had been laid upon him, and they were safe from His ignorance of their affairs. He continued digging until he uncovered swords and shields that had long been buried in Zamzam. When the Quraysh saw this, they said: "Give us a share of what you have found." He replied: "It belongs to the House of God." He dug on until the water welled up; he then contained it so that it would not overflow, and built a basin over it.

Zamzam is the well of Ismail ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him. It is narrated that during a year of drought, Ismail was suffering from thirst with his mother Hajar; she sought refuge in God and called upon Him, and Allah caused the spring of Zamzam to well up before them. When it later fell into disuse, it was buried, and what had been placed in it was buried with it — until the excavation of 'Abd al-Muttalib.

Concerning 'Abd al-Muttalib's excavation of Zamzam, Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza says:

> *I say — and what shall I say of him because of this? —*
> *to you, O Ibn Salma: you are the digger of Zamzam.*
> *The excavation of Ibrahim on the day of Hajar's son,*
> *and the running of Jibril in the age of Adam.*

It is said that 'Abd al-Muttalib found a golden gazelle among the buried items and greatly admired it. He cast lots over it with arrows — some for the House and some for himself — and the arrow of the House came out, so he adorned the House with it. It was the first ornament with which the House was ever adorned.

It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him: when the Quraysh saw what 'Abd al-Muttalib had brought forth from Zamzam, they gathered around him and said: "O 'Abd al-Muttalib, this is the well of our father Ishmael, and we have a right to it — let us share in it and in whatever you find." He said: "I will not do that, for this is a matter that was entrusted to me alone and not to you, and He granted it to me from among you." They refused to accept this unless he shared it with them, saying: "Our judge in this shall be such-and-such." He agreed to take the matter before the soothsayer of Bani Sa'd ibn Hudhaym.

He set out with them, and each tribe of the Quraysh sent one man. The land at that time was waterless; as they made their way through one of those parched stretches between the Hijaz and the Levant, the water ran out for 'Abd al-Muttalib and his companions. He asked the other tribes of Quraysh for water, but they refused, saying: "We are ourselves in want, and we fear for ourselves what has befallen you." Seeing no other course, they dismounted. Each man dug a pit and sat in it, agreeing: "Whoever among us dies first shall be buried by those who remain." Then 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "By Allah, it is weakness and surrender to simply sit here and wait for death without striking the earth in search of water." He rose, mounted his camel, and when it got up from beneath him, water burst forth from under its resting place — a sweet spring. 'Abd al-Muttalib dismounted, gave thanks and drank deeply.

He and his companions drank and filled their water-skins. Then he called to those tribes of Quraysh who were with him and said: "Come to the water — Allah has provided us with water." They came and drank, and then they said: "By Allah, Allah has already given His judgment for you against us, O 'Abd al-Muttalib. We shall never dispute with you again over Zamzam. Whoever gave you water from this camel in the wilderness is your waterman of Zamzam — go back and tend your watering as its rightful master." So he returned, and they returned, and he was set apart from them in this matter.

This is among the virtues that one mentions not to boast, but because it speaks to the truth of his visions — for what he saw concerning Zamzam was a clear sign of Allah's favour and of what Allah had singled him out for. As the Prophet, may God bless him and his family, said: "A true vision is one of twenty-six parts of prophecy."

And what he was then shown — the appearance of the water in Zamzam, the well of Ishmael, peace be upon him — was a blessing for him: Allah provided him with water, caused it to spring from the earth for him, and made it a miracle witnessed by all his people, one that none among them could deny or diminish.

'Abd al-Muttalib was the finest of the Quraysh, their chief, and their master. In him the light of prophecy was visible, along with the majesty of kingship, the awe of virtue, and his qualities are beyond enumeration. He was called "Sayyid al-Wadi" — the Master of the Valley — meaning Mecca and its surroundings.

edits.chapter_key: the tree that came when called
edits.body_md:
Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat was a relative by marriage to the Quraysh; he had a wife, the daughter of a lion — Ibn Abd al-Ar'i — and he would bring her to Mecca and stay there for a period with the followers of her people. He had close ties with them, and he was a poet. He sent them a poem urging them to cease from war, exhorting them to follow the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, reminding them of what God had done for them and how He had turned away from them the army of the elephant and its cunning stratagem. He said:

> *Luay ibn Ghalib is not unaware of me —*
> *any traveler, whether he offered or reported.*
>
> *Concerning the distant ones — they grieve that we stand*
> *with the article of a man who has taken care of his own among you.*
>
> *And I did not free myself of my needs and views of it,*
> *and I had a groom burdened with worries.*
>
> *She has the finest of endings and the woodcutter —*
> *you silence two on every kiss.*
>
> *And the evil of your deceit and the treading of scorpions —*
> *may God protect you from the evil of your deeds.*
>
> *The pain of the healers has struck it rightly,*
> *and the morals are shown and the soundness of private counsel —*
> *and the replacement of the sacred garment of the antelope.*
>
> *So he reminded them of God at first glance —*
> *war is departing from you in greetings.*
>
> *And tell them, for God rules with His wisdom —*
> *it is the dependence for the two allies or for the kin.*
>
> *Hopes — send them, send them reproach,*
> *and acquit the Sadeef from the hump and the stranger.*
> *It severs a soul and destroys a nation —*
> *Shella, and the echoes of the warrior's garb.*
>
> *Or replace it with warming afterward,*
> *as though the eyes of locusts had purchased it,*
> *with musk and the dust of kagur.*
>
> *In its days, and knowledge is the knowledge of warfare,*
> *and a basin and tents of water — the bitter stripes —*
> *with the outcome of a loyal companion's mother.*
>
> *The people among you are on the right path —*
> *do you consider it, or was there a war of wood?*
> *Did you not know that there is no war*
> *for the one of great provision, a guest who is not turned away?*
>
> *How many a nobleman, Maswad, has been wounded by it,*
> *and this is pure charisma — the cream of the deliberate.*
> *Great are the embers of fire — he is praised,*
> *the vitality of youth broadcast with him,*
>
> *and the water of the rocky stream in the crags, as though —*
> *concerning war, in its advance and its aftermath,*
> *he tells how many people are right about her —*
> *your reckoning, I swear, by the finest of reckoners.*
>
> *So they sold the spears to a warrior and remembered:*
> *you have a guardian other than the Lord of the piercings.*
> *A man confused by a religion — it must not be so —*
> *we have a purpose that the melts may guide.*
>
> *Establish for us a true religion, for you*
> *are the faithful, and dreams are not isolated things.*
> *And I pay tribute to these people — light and infallibility —*
> *bands guided by bands.*
>
> *The seeker sees needs drawing toward your homes*
> *in any case — the finest people of the brow.*
> *The nations have known that your secrets*
> *are what I state truly in the midst of the processions,*
>
> *and I favor it in my view, and above it is a year's standing*
> *in the corners of this House among the trees.*
> *So arise, single out your Lord and be anointed —*
> *the day after Abu Yakhsum, the guide of the battalions.*
>
> *You have a warning from him — believe it —*
> *so do not worry, for war will not ensnare you;*
> *it is adorned for people, and then they see it.*
>
> *Burn — do not grill the weak — and step down.*
> *If you do not know war, then ask,*
> *and I shall be rewarded if people do not grasp the essence.*
>
> *You have the navel of al-Batha', smelling of rabbits,*
> *a polished lineage without flaw —*
> *you preserve the ancient dignities of nobility,*
> *on the slingers at the heads of the virtues —*
> *his battalion is easy to touch and his leg,*
> *Jude al-Malik between Saf and Hasib.*
> *When the victory of the Lord of the Throne came to you, he saw them:*
> *to his family there is no one but Asaib.*
> *Hurry, Harin — and he does not repent.*
> *He lives by it, the saying of a man who is no liar.*
> *If you perish, you will perish, and the seasons will perish.*

When the Quraysh were discouraged from rallying the Arabs to support him, they refrained from speaking directly against the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, resorting instead to harming him with their tongues, even as his uncle Abu Talib stood in his defense. Meanwhile, the Prophet called them to Allah the Almighty, reciting to them the verses of His Book that had been revealed to him. Yet they persisted in their disbelief and denial, stubbornly rejecting the signs that were shown to them.

The following is narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, in one of his sermons. He said:

"I was with him, may Allah bless him and his family, when the Quraysh came to him. They said: 'O Muhammad, you have made a great claim that neither your fathers nor any of your kinsmen ever made. We will put a matter to you, and if you show it to us and answer it, we will know that you are a prophet and messenger. If you cannot, we will know that you are a lying sorcerer.'

He said to them: 'What do you ask?'

They said: 'Call this tree to come to you, so that it uproots itself and stands before you.'

He said: 'Allah is Able over all things. If Allah does this for you, will you believe and bear witness to the truth?'

They said: Yes.

He said: 'I will show you what you ask, and I know full well that you will not turn to what is good — for among you are those in whose hearts it has been sealed, and those who are partisan.'

Then he said: 'O tree, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day, and you know that I am the Messenger of Allah, then uproot yourself and stand before me.'

By Him who sent him with the truth, it uprooted itself with a great rushing sound, thundering like the beating wings of a bird, until it stood in the hands of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, and flung its upper branch toward him, while one of its branches grazed my forehead — for I was standing at his right hand.

When the people saw this, they said: 'Arrogance and sorcery!'

They asked that half of it return. He commanded it, and half of it came back as though it had never moved. Then it drew closer still until it nearly encircled the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, and they said: 'Command it to return the other half as well.' So he commanded it, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, and it returned.

I said: 'There is no god but Allah. I am the first to believe in you, O Messenger of Allah, and the first to acknowledge that the tree did what it did by the command of Allah, exalted be He, as a testament to your prophethood and in reverence for your word.'

Yet all the people said: 'He is a lying sorcerer — and sorcery is well-suited to his kind. Is there no one who will believe you in your claim except someone like this?' — meaning me.

And I am among those people whom you do not blame regarding Allah, especially the righteous — those whose words are the words of the righteous, who spend their nights in worship and their days in journey, holding fast to the rope of the Quran. They follow the Sunnah of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger; they are neither arrogant nor conceited nor haughty. Their hearts are tender and their bodies are at work!"

This is the saying of the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him.

The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, showed them mighty signs — among them the splitting of the moon, and other things beyond the power of all humankind — yet they only grew more arrogant, and their denial and disbelief only deepened.

The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, reached out to those in the Arab lands — the Jews, the Christians, their scholars, monks, and rabbis — and they came to him to hear his arguments. Some of them recognized in him the evidence of prophethood from what they found in their books: they submitted to him and to what pointed to his nature, and their knowledge of him. Yet when they returned, most of them spoke of him only under the shadow of envy and enmity, which prevented them from acknowledging his prophethood, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family.

Islam spread and news of the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, became known across the horizons, and hearts inclined toward it. Many things happened in this period that would take long to recount. Abu Talib warned the Quraysh sternly against their denial of him and said, in part:

> *Wake up, O Banu Ghalib, and be forewarned —*
> *outstanding men from your own house will face you.*
> *Otherwise, I fear what may come upon you.*
> *By the Lord of the West and the East,*
> *let your forebears be a lesson to you:*
> *Thamud and 'Ad — who remains of them*
> *after they tasted what came before you?*
> *The she-camel of the Throne when she was watered —*
> *the next day they hamstrung her.*
> *From Allah came a blow from the blue,*
> *Hasama from India — the Rotaq.*
> *So wrath descended upon them.*
> *The next day he severed her hock —*
> *wonders in the desert laid bare —*
> *for those who are patient, truthful, and pious.*
> *And I am more awed by that than you,*
> *by the hand of one who has risen through hardship*
> *in spite of this foolish opposition.*
> *So Allah held him in His palm:*
> *He dissolved the seduction and they would not believe it —*
> *I will outfox your obstinate one when he is beguiled.*

It is related by "the Sticky Stone": "When the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, had made his command firm and openly proclaimed the worship of his Lord, he would come to the House and pray there. Abu Jahl ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi came upon him one day while he was praying, stood up, and seized a stone, filling both hands with it. He advanced toward the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, as he was prostrating, intending to strike his head — all this after the disbelievers of the Quraysh had incited him against him, and they sat watching to see what he would do. But when he drew close to the Prophet while he was prostrating, he recoiled, his face drained of color, and he cast the stone away from his hand. The people stood up to him and said: 'What is the matter with you, O Abu al-Hakam?'

He said: 'When I drew near him, a great stallion camel loomed before me, opening its mouth — and I fled from it.' They said to one another: 'By Allah, Muhammad has been safeguarded against us, as no man among a people before him was ever safeguarded.'"

edits.chapter_key: hamza, umar, and the parchment in the ka'bah
edits.body_md:
Islam was spreading and growing in numbers. Then the Prophet's uncle, Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, accepted Islam. The occasion was this: Abu Jahl had abused and cursed the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, and news of this reached Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. He entered the mosque in a rage, not pausing for anything, until he stood over Abu Jahl as he sat among his people. Hamza raised his bow and struck him a severe blow on the head, then said: "You dare to curse my nephew while I follow his religion? I am the uncle of the Messenger of God." The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, came and heard what had happened, and he declared his acceptance of Islam.

Hamza, may God be pleased with him, addressed Abu Jahl in verse about what he had done:

> *Abu Jahl was shaken by what we had brought upon him.*
> *By your unjust command — act on it if you will.*
>
> *You harmed the Messenger of God — we have forbidden*
> *your unjust decree, though you persist.*
>
> *You face our defiance in spite of what you have done;*
> *had you sought God, you would not have been brought low.*
>
> *You turned from truth when it was offered to you;*
> *you were destroyed before destruction came.*
>
> *You harmed the Messenger of God and have been led astray;*
> *I could not live after they returned.*
>
> *Until we made you taste humiliation,*
> *souls were healed, and we found our cure.*

Among the most harmful of the polytheists were Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him, prayed that God would guide one of the two to Islam, so that religion would be strengthened and its corruptors diminished.

One day, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab set out with his sword, declaring that he intended to kill Muhammad — the man who, as he saw it, had split the Quraysh, corrupted their thinking, disparaged their religion, and reviled their gods. He came to where the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, was sitting in a gathering of his companions.

He knocked at the door. When those inside heard his voice, one of the companions of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, rose and peered through the door. Seeing who it was, he went back to the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, and told him. Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "Let him in — if he means harm, we will kill him with his own sword." The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, said: "Admit him."

The Messenger of God rose to receive him in the room. He took hold of 'Umar by his garment, then seized him firmly and said: "What has brought you here, Ibn al-Khattab? I think God will send down a punishment upon you from heaven." 'Umar replied: "I have come to accept Islam, O Messenger of God." The color returned to the Prophet's face and his trembling ceased, and 'Umar submitted.

When news of 'Umar's Islam reached the Muslims in Abyssinia, they said: "'Umar would never surrender unless even his donkey submitted" — meaning they knew how deeply he had been set against Islam and how fiercely he had hated the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family.

When the Quraysh saw that the Negus had shielded the emigrants from them, and that Abu Talib continued to protect the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, and that his uncle Hamza had embraced Islam with all that had been mentioned, and that those who remained Muslim enjoyed protection such that no harm could easily reach them, they despaired of winning Arab support against him. They gathered, turned every scheme over, debated every option, and in the end saw no recourse but to draw up a document binding the Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib — pledging that no one would marry them, sell to them, or deal with them. They wrote this document, made a solemn pact upon what it contained, and hung it inside the hollow of the Ka'bah. Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib withdrew to Abu Talib ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, entered his quarter, and stood with him.

Abu Lahab 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, however, broke from Banu Hashim and went over to Banu 'Abd Shams and those among the Quraysh who openly declared their disbelief. The Banu 'Abd Shams praised him for it, and Hind bint 'Utbah welcomed him, saying: "Well done, son of 'Utbah! You have supported the cause and distanced yourself from those who turned away." She said: "Yes, may God reward you well, O Abu 'Utbah."

Abu Talib said concerning their pact:

> *Have you not carried my message to Luwayy?*
> *Truly — carry a message sent in earnest.*
>
> *Our elder cousins are bound to us,*
> *and our brothers from 'Abd Shams and Nawfal —*
> *yet they rose against us,*
> *drawn by a seductive order of enticement and deceit.*
>
> *Nawasi Hashim yielded to humiliation?*
> *They say: if we kill Muhammad —*
> *in Mecca, the proclamation in every quarter —*
> *you have lied! By the House of God, he is in our keeping,*
> *with his blood-right and the corner of the manumission.*
>
> *By pilgrimage or by the one whose throat was cut at the Nayb —*
> *defenders who free every bone and joint.*
>
> *You will reach him only over our bodies;*
> *prayers in the hollow of the wide valley.*
>
> *You call for mercy while you have been unjust —*
> *either well, or in the end hastened.*
>
> *Wait, and when tomorrow's war brings its result,*
> *you will learn who it is you have wronged.*
>
> *When we pass through it with our swords*
> *on a rise at the head of the lofty mountain —*
>
> *and Muhammad received the spring of the Abtah,*
> *Ka'b's noble pair after the first —*
>
> *and Hashim sheltered him, for Hashim*
> *casts aside whatever would bend and wither —*
>
> *if you wish to kill Muhammad,*
> *and the fluid one is the rock of the sanctuary,*
> *we will defend him with all our might,*
> *and he is like the lightning-flash of a cloud, a cleaver.*
>
> *And all my fighting men thirst to follow his heels,*
> *Dalas, like Zahaz of the revolving springs,*
> *and every charging rider overflowing with resolve.*
>
> *I believe I smell from the wolves of Hashim*
> *men who meet heroes in every quarter,*
> *and the finest lords of men in every trial —*
> *they are the masters of chieftains in every land.*
>
> *Luwayy, a multitude from the sons of Ka'b —*
> *shall I not report it to my own soul among us?*
>
> *A prophet like Moses, inscribed at the opening of books,*
> *and better than what God has singled out with love.*
>
> *And for him is love among God's servants,*
> *and what you have fabricated in your document —*
> *you have a creature that writhes like a serpent,*
> *and one who has no longing becomes savage as a wolf.*
>
> *Awake, awake, before the wealthy are struck down;*
> *we were bound together in affection and closeness.*
>
> *Do not follow the command of the schemer who cuts ties —*
> *a command for those who have tasted the war of Aleppo,*
> *and you enter a war of allies and perhaps*
> *consolation from the bite of time, and no anguish.*
>
> *We and the Lord of the House surrender Ahmad.*

He also said in this regard:

> *Did you not know that we have found Muhammad?*
> *And the hands of the witnesses were filled with resolve,*
> *with it and the wall of flesh — they drink of it.*
> *It is as though the horses stand firm in their rocky ground,*
> *and the cavalry of fierce battle.*
>
> *He commended his daughter to stabbing and striking.*
> *Is not our father Hashim strong of arm?*
> *We do not lament what comes upon us in calamity,*
> *nor do we tire of war until it is satisfied.*
>
> *If the souls of the truffles flew away in terror,*
> *we would find the people of blood-right and sanctuary.*
>
> *And when you raise stories against us,*
> *in the battle of your wrongdoing you will see the breaking of the cane.*

Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, peace be upon him, said concerning the parchment and what the people had unanimously agreed upon:

> *Time passes, and those we love depart —*
> *are the people not struck with wonder?*
>
> *With shamelessness and aggression without cause,*
> *and the words of people whose minds I have lost faith in —*
> *to speak a fool's word or a sign of defect.*
>
> *They say: we shall starve Ahmad out.*
> *Messages of truth and a revelation that is not false —*
> *he came with clear truth and established it.*
>
> *Worshippers who have right and love in God,*
> *letters from the One of Might, to stand in line.*
>
> *To you — and the word of the noble messengers:*
> *if you accept what has come from your Lord,*
> *and during war, the war of kinsmen is grievous,*
> *you will not be disgraced before any traveler.*
>
> *Do not think we will abandon Muhammad as Muslims*
> *without striking brow and forehead.*
>
> *May God have mercy on us, and exalt his neighborhood —*
> *be dazzled by our gathering.*
>
> *Noble Luwayy ibn Ghalib,*
> *and a branch from Hashim, by whom he was known.*
>
> *Wait, and when war breaks out in our house,*
> *the people of the quarter will scatter after their gathering,*
> *and some people will be humbled, left exposed.*
>
> *Basha'a means every leader and follower;*
> *Fayel reveals the servants of the Kaaba's keepers.*
> *They have been struck with an eternity of many trials.*

The Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib remained under the boycott for three years, without contracting marriages or conducting trade, with food reaching them only in secret.

Hakim ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid ibn Asad frequently sent food to Banu Hashim in general, and to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, in particular, out of regard for his aunt Khadijah bint Khuwaylid and her bond with the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family. Hakim was a man of sound judgment, wealth, standing, and protection among the Quraysh. He would send caravan after caravan by night, and the people of Banu Hashim would meet him and take what he brought.

One night Abu Jahl ibn Hisham intercepted him and confronted him, saying: "Are you going with food to Banu Hashim? I swear, you and your food shall not pass until I have exposed you before all of Mecca." Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham ibn al-Harith ibn Asad came upon them and said: "What is this?" Abu Jahl said: "He is carrying food to Banu Hashim." Abu al-Bakhtari said to him: "Rather, this is food belonging to his aunt that she had with him — he is sending it to her. Are you going to prevent a man from bringing food to his aunt? Get out of this man's way." Abu Jahl leapt at him, and Abu al-Bakhtari struck him with a camel's jawbone, landing a severe blow. Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib witnessed this not long after, and Abu Jahl hated that the companions of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, should come to hear of it, so they kept it quiet and mocked him in silence.

The Messenger of Allah called upon his people day and night, openly and in secret, summoning them to the command of Allah without fearing anyone in doing so. The Quraysh, when Allah shielded him from them, found that his uncle and his kinsmen of Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib stood between them and their desire to oppress him. So they resorted to mocking him, his family, and his companions.

Among those who did so were Abu Lahab and his wife Umm Jamil bint Harb ibn Umayyah, who is described in the Quran as the "carrier of firewood." It was said that she used to gather thorny wood and scatter it along the path of the Messenger of Allah wherever he would walk. It was also said that she used to spread slander. Allah knows best.

Allah then revealed concerning them:

> ﴿ تَبَّتْ يَدَا أَبِي لَهَبٍ وَتَبَّ ۝ مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ ﴾
> "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he. His wealth availed him nothing, nor what he earned." (al-Masad: 1–2)

— to the end of the surah.

When she heard what had been revealed about her, Umm Jamil came while the Messenger of Allah was sitting in the mosque near the Ka'bah, with Abu Bakr beside him. She had a piece of stone in her hand and said: "O Abu Bakr, I have heard what your companion has said about me":

> *We have disobeyed, and his son commanded him,*
> *and his religion is contemptible.*

"And I was kept from seeing the Messenger of Allah."

The Quraysh used to call the Messenger of Allah by an insulting name, cursing him. But the Messenger of Allah said to his companions: "Does it not amaze you how Allah has turned the harm of the Quraysh away from me? They curse and revile a man they call 'the reproachable one,' and I am Muhammad."

Abu Talib addressed Abu Lahab, reproaching him for withdrawing from Banu Hashim and appealing to him:

> *The dreams of nations have left you in foolishness —*
> *I marveled, O Ibn Shayba, at what has come to pass.*
> *They say whoever seeks Muhammad shall regret it —*
> *do something other than evil, or draw near.*
> *Yet close to you there is none who stands in rank,*
> *only the envious one who harbors treachery.*
> *A man has come from the finest of the sons of Manaf —*
> *do not ride against him from among them.*
> *Be a man of solidarity and honor,*
> *and do not abandon him so long as I live and breathe.*
> *Their loyalty among people is the finest of all —*
> *enemies defend the heights of the Hashimites.*
> *Not through an oath nor through addition —*
> *if he has kinship, you have a bond of honor.*
> *He sails across the encircling seas,*
> *yet he is of Hashim at its very core.*
>
> *A minister over enemies who goes unguarded —*
> *rally all people away from him and stand by him.*
> *Our cousins, are you too weak?*
> *If the Quraysh are angry with him, tell them:*
> *how do they deceive us under cover of darkness?*
> *And how the wombs among them hold a hollow.*
> *We did not wrong the people with injustice,*
> *nor were we light in what they did to them.*
> *But we were the hope of the guardians and the sanctuary,*
> *and glory in the sight of the great ones fills us.*

Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad sought the protection of Abu Talib against his own people, Banu Makhzum, who wished to kill him. Abu Talib protected him, so they came to Abu Talib and said: "O Abu Talib, you have prevented us from your nephew Muhammad — so why do you also prevent us from our own man?" He said: "He has sought my protection, and he is my sister's son. If I did not protect my nephew, I would not protect my brother's son." They argued with him over this, and Abu Lahab rose and said to them: "O assembly of Quraysh, you have burdened this elder beyond measure — you keep pressing upon him in the presence of his own people. By Allah, either step back from this matter or stand with him in what he has done, until he reaches what he seeks." They said: "We will withdraw from you and from what you dislike, O Abu Utbah." And they had, in that, a guardian and a supporter for the Messenger of Allah.

When Abu Talib heard what he had heard, he was moved, and he composed verses inciting Abu Lahab to support the Messenger of Allah:

> *Turn around the nursling — for no sooner are grievances raised*
> *than Abu Mutab, your darkness stands firm.*
> *To him I say: where has my counsel gone?*
> *Do you dishonor it, or have the seasons fallen away?*
> *Do not accept a time when I have not devised a plan —*
> *you were not created for helplessness.*
> *The paths of weakness lie elsewhere.*
> *The brother of war gives regret until they find safety.*
> *Fight — war is ordained — and you shall not see*
> *them strip you as a spoiler or one who spoils.*
> *And how have they not gained anything great from you.*
> *And orphans — orphans in their stubbornness —*
> *may Allah requite Abd Shams and Nawfal*
> *for scattering our group after friendship and affection.*
> *They lingered and tasted corruption all together,*
> *obeying Ibn Dhakwan, Qays, and Disma.*
> *And when you see a day the people rise up,*
> *a woman — Abu Utayba is his uncle —*
> *you lied, and the House of God is offended by Muhammad.*

Hisham ibn Amr ibn al-Harith then moved to have the document annulled — the document the Quraysh had drawn up against Banu Hashim. He was a man of standing among his people and was among those who kept watch over Banu Hashim. Having done this for a long time, he went to Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, then to al-Mut'im ibn Adi ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf, then to Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, then to Zama'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad.

They gathered and met at the head of the pilgrim track by night, and they said: "We eat food, we wear clothes, we take wives in marriage, yet the sons of Hashim — nothing is sold to them nor bought from them, they cannot marry nor be given in marriage." They then made a pact and agreed to repudiate the document. Zuhayr said: "I will start by speaking and be the first among you."

The next morning, Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah circled the Ka'bah seven times, then came to the people and said: "O people of Mecca — we eat food and wear clothes, while the Banu Hashim perish: nothing is sold to them, nothing is bought from them. I swear I will not sit until this unjust and contemptible document is torn apart."

Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who was in a corner of the mosque, said: "You lie — by the House of God, it shall not be torn." Zama'ah ibn al-Aswad said: "You — by Allah — are the liar. We did not approve of this document when it was written." Abu al-Bakhtari said: "Zama'ah speaks the truth — we are not satisfied with what is written in it." Al-Mut'im ibn Adi said: "You both speak the truth, and whoever says otherwise lies. We disavow before Allah what is written in it." Hisham ibn Amr said the same. Abu Jahl said: "This is a matter that was decided overnight" — meaning it had been arranged without him.

The Messenger of Allah said to his uncle Abu Talib: "O uncle, my Lord has sent a small creature against the document of the Quraysh, and it has eaten away every name of Allah that was in it, leaving only the injustice, the severance of ties, and the falsehood in it. Allah has informed me of this."

When Abu Talib heard this, he went to where the Quraysh were gathered at the side of the mosque and said: "O assembly of Quraysh, my nephew has told me such-and-such — so bring out your document. If it is as he has described, then cease your boycott against us."

The people said: "We are satisfied." They agreed to this, then examined the document — and found it exactly as the Messenger of Allah had said.

When the document was torn and what it contained was annulled, Abu Talib composed verses about it:

> *By their faces — I swear by God — people resolve*
> *that they came to our sea for the work of our Lord.*
> *And all that does not please God is destined to corrupt —*
> *he tells them the document has been torn apart.*
> *Untangled, its knots undone, its spell assembled —*
> *those who would not crack it fell before it.*
> *The magic of the end of ages could not prevail;*
> *its strands wavered about its head.*
> *To cut from it an arm and sever its limb —*
> *it was enough that this befell it in full.*
> *Their quarry thunders in fear of misfortune,*
> *and they drive the people of the two sanctuaries to flight.*
> *Which of them at that moment shall be saved?*
> *Let the plower turn his course around.*
> *It has an arrow, a bow, and its string —*
> *and you rise between the two woods as scribes.*
> *So we fortified ourselves in the heart of Mecca —*
> *who will be driven from the civilization of Mecca?*
> *We did not yield; we shall increase in goodness and gratitude,*
> *we grew up in it while its people were few.*
> *If you would freeze the hands of those who would overflow,*
> *and feed until people leave behind their bounty,*
> *may God reward you — O pilgrims — in succession,*
> *may He guide firmly and lead aright.*
> *Bound together — yet they are stripped and united,*
> *sitting at the head of the pilgrim track, most resolute.*
> *If he does not walk in the fold of the shield, I am lost —*
> *every falcon helped her as though she were*
> *a burning brand, enough to blaze.*
> *Bold enough to make the engagements as though —*
> *if his face wearies, his face shall turn out*
> *from the most noble of Luay ibn Ghalib.*
> *Long and sharp, half his leg protruding —*
> *on his face the clouds water and are glad.*
> *He summons the summer quarters and mobilizes —*
> *shelter me, O clan companions of Salih.*
> *And he grows greatly wherever he stood against the enemy,*
> *so we ranged across the land and paved the way*
> *slowly, while the rest of the people slept.*
> *Repel the enemy — nothing else avails —*
> *the great commander has given his order, then praise.*
> *Preserve this reconciliation, every justification —*
> *and the best of people, Muhammad, was pleased with it.*
> *They returned — Sahl ibn Baydha among the pleased —*
> *and we used to be content before that.*
> *What is the association with nations in most of our affairs?*
> *Attain what you seek and do not hesitate —*
> *we are elders; we do not accept darkness.*
> *Do you have something to offer tomorrow?*
> *By al-Qusay — do you have something in your mouth?*
> *A great lord, master and son of a master —*
> *they spent what they spent in their nights, and became.*
> *You have milk — if you speak, it is pure.*
> *I and you are as he said.*

Abu Talib also said concerning the document:

> *And the people of steadfastness from your many people —*
> *are those who hold a station at the end of the night*
> *not to be crowded away from their rightful struggle.*
> *And look — see it from Luay ibn Ghalib:*
> *he is a wreck yet no guilty man.*
> *If the commander devised a plan within it,*
> *and an ancient religion whose people are not let down —*
> *and he who calls to Allah alone has not been deceived,*
> *and if he can nurture the people, he shall nurture them,*
> *and he who calls to righteousness and meets it has not withered.*
> *And there is no one who knows a matter like one who has tried it —*
> *those who have tried in the past know they are not in a position.*
> *When the absent one is reported, the people grow fond —*
> *the document held a lesson.*
> *And they did not take revenge from the one who speaks the truth, though he is vindicated —*
> *may God erase from it their disbelief and disobedience.*
> *And whoever invents what is not true is a liar,*
> *and what they said has been rendered void.*
> *Upon the disgruntled among our people — none to be blamed —*
> *so Ibn Abdullah has become a believer among us.*
> *We are estranged from us, yet not truly distant —*
> *so do not think, Muhammad, that we are losers.*
> *His standing among the people is the finest standing —*
> *a hand of Hashim will protect him from us.*
> *By the people of al-Uqair, or by the people of Yathrib,*
> *Talih is in the palm of the harvest.*
> *So the one who challenged every light —*
> *let us swear, a hero, with the ancient and veiled.*
> *By God the truth — He has confirmed us in it and we were not*
> *among those who spread lies about the close prophet.*
> *You leave him until you fight all around him —*
> *when we are unjustly driven from people, we grow angry.*
> *O our people, do not oppress us — for we*
> *do not depart from your counsel in every direction.*
> *And cease your curiosity about your dreams —*
> *so reward you with weakness in mother and father.*
> *And do not set upon us with darkness and harm,*
> *for God — who is his God — shall help him.*

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his family then went to the Arabs, presenting Islam to them, seeking their support during the pilgrimage seasons and urging people toward their lands.

This is narrated with a chain of transmission from the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, who said:

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was instructed to present himself to the Arab tribes during the pilgrimage seasons, he set out for that purpose and ordered me to accompany him, so I went out with him. Abu Bakr — a man of deep knowledge of lineage — went out with him too. We made our way to a gathering of people, and Abu Bakr stepped forward to address them.

He said: "Who are these people?" They said: "From Rabi'ah." He said: "Are you from her nobles, or from those who were defeated by her?" They said: "From her nobles." He said: "And who among her nobles are you?" They said: "The mightiest of the mighty." He said: "Is your strength 'Awf ibn Muhamalim, who used to say, 'Awf ibn Muhamalim, is there no generosity in Wadi Auf?'" They said: "No." He said: "Are you Bastam ibn Qays, the magnanimous one, the pride of the living?" They said: "No." He said: "Are you Jassas ibn Murrah, the defender of honor and the protector of the neighbor?" They said: "No." He said: "Are you the son of Shreek, the slayer of kings and the one who put them to the test?" They said: "No." He said: "Are you the one who bears the unique crown?" They said: "No." He said: "Are you the uncles of kings from Kindah?" They said: "No." He then said: "Are you the sons-in-law of the kings of the flesh?" They said: "No." He said: "Then you are not the eldest wonder, nor the wonder of the youngest."

At that, a man from Bani Shayban with a lowly bearing rose to face him; he was known as Daghl. He said:

"The burden we neither know nor carry — our questioner must ask elsewhere."

"You there — you have questioned us while we put our questions to you. Do not conceal it from us: who is this man?" He said: "From Quraysh." He said: "A fine people of honor and leadership. And from which branch of Quraysh?" He said: "From Bani Taym ibn Murrah." He said: "I swear by Allah, the Thrower, you come from the very same threshing floor. Do you know that Qusai ibn Kilab ibn Murrah gathered the tribes of Fihr and was called al-Mujammi'?" He said: "No." He said: "Are you Hashim, who crumbled bread for his people and fed the pilgrims?" He said: "No." He said: "Are you Shaybah al-Hamd — 'Abd al-Muttalib — whose face shone like a moon in the deep darkness?" He said: "No." He said: "Who then are you from among the overflowing people?" He said: "No." He said: "Are you from the people of the council?" He said: "No." He then said: "Are you from the people of al-Rifadah?" He said: "No." He said: "Are you from the people of the hijab?" He said: "No." He said: "Are you from the people of the watering?" He said: "No."

At that, Abu Bakr pulled the reins of his camel and turned back toward the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. The man called after him — meaning something to the effect that the flood had been diverted, pushed away, digested by force, or split — and said: "By Allah, if I had stood my ground I would have told you that you are one of the fools of Quraysh — or what else would you be? A Badghug."

Ali, peace be upon him, said: When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, heard this, he smiled. I said to Abu Bakr: "I have found you to have fallen into a fool among the Arabs." He said: "Yes, O Abu al-Hasan — for every affliction there is a greater affliction, and the affliction of wit is entrusted to logic."

Then we rode on to another gathering with composure and dignity. Abu Bakr went forward to greet the people, and they returned his greeting. He said: "Who are these people?" They said: "From Shayban ibn Rabi'ah." Abu Bakr turned to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and said: "By my father and my mother, there is no greater glory to be found among their people." Among those gathered were Mafruq ibn 'Amr, Hani' ibn Qabisah, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha, and al-Nu'man ibn Shreek. Mafruq ibn 'Amr was the most commanding of them in speech and the most eloquent of tongue; he had two locks of hair that fell onto his chest, and the ears of the people in that gathering were turned toward Abu Bakr.

Abu Bakr said to him: "How many are you?" He said: "We number in the thousands, and a thousand are not overwhelmed by a small force." He said: "And how strong is your defense?" He said: "We spare no effort, and every people has its mettle." He said: "And how do you fare in war against your enemy?" He said: "We are the most fierce in the press of battle. When we are stirred to anger, we drive our horses over our children, preferring the weapon above all else. Victory comes from Allah — sometimes for us and sometimes against us. Yet perhaps you are the brother of Quraysh?" He said: "If the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, has reached you" — and he pointed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him — "this is he." He said: "We have heard that this is what he says."

He drew near to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and said: "To what do you call, O brother of Quraysh?"

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I call you to bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that I, Muhammad, am the Messenger of Allah; and to protect me and defend me and support me. The Quraysh have set themselves against the command of Allah, denied His Messenger, and clung to falsehood over truth — except those whom Allah has protected and guided to His religion. Allah is the Protector and the Sufficient."

He said: "And to what else do you call, O brother of Quraysh? All that is in the earth" — meaning: if these words were from their own, we would have recognized them. So he recited to them, may Allah bless him and his family:

> ﴿ تَعَالَوْا أَتْلُ مَا حَرَّمَ رَبُّكُمْ عَلَيْكُمْ ﴾
> "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you," to the Almighty's words: "This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may use reason." (al-An'am: 151)

He said: "And what else do you call for?"

He recited to them:

> ﴿ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِالْعَدْلِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ وَإِيتَاءِ ذِي الْقُرْبَىٰ وَيَنْهَىٰ عَنِ الْفَحْشَاءِ وَالْمُنكَرِ وَالْبَغْيِ ﴾
> "Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression — He admonishes you, that perhaps you will take heed." (al-Nahl: 90)

Mafruq ibn 'Amr said: "You call to the noblest of character and the finest of deeds. Yet some people have come out against you and denied you." As though he wished to draw Hani' ibn Qabisah into the conversation, he said: "This is Hani' ibn Qabisah, our elder and the custodian of our religion."

Hani' ibn Qabisah spoke and said: "O brother of Quraysh, we have heard your words, and we find that for us to abandon our religion and embrace yours in a single sitting — a sitting in which you have not fully set out your case — and without seeing what the outcome of what you invite us to will bring, would be a slip of judgment, a hasty conclusion, and a misfortune for those behind us who would hate to have a binding agreement made without their counsel. Let us return and let you return, and we will reflect and consider." As though he wished to draw al-Muthanna ibn Haritha into the conversation, he said: "This is al-Muthanna ibn Haritha, our elder, our chief, and the master of our wars." So al-Muthanna ibn Haritha spoke and said: "O brother of Quraysh, I have heard your words, and the answer — as for leaving our religion and embracing yours — that would be a fine answer. But the answer is that we dwell between two streams: that of Khusraw and that of the Arabs."

The Messenger of Allah said to him: "What are these two streams?" He replied: The waters of the Arabs and the rivers of Khusraw. As for what lies along the waters of the Arabs — the sin of one's companion there is forgiven and his excuse accepted; but as for what lies along the rivers of Khusraw — the fault rests entirely with its owner, who is neither forgiven nor excused. We went down there under a covenant we made with Khusraw: we cause no disturbance and we take no independent action. Yet what you call us to — that which kings despise — if you wish us to shelter you and support you in it, then after the waters of the Arabs, we will give you victory and aid.

The Prophet replied: "You have done no wrong in your answer, since you spoke truthfully. Only one who embraces the religion of Allah in all its dimensions truly fulfills it. But tell me — if Allah grants you their wealth, their homes, and their women, will you praise and glorify Him?" He said: That would be for you, O Messenger of Allah. The Messenger of Allah then said to them: "We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of glad tidings, and a warner, and a caller to Allah by His permission and a shining light." (al-Ahzab)

He then rose and took my hand and said: "O Ali — these are the dreams of the pre-Islamic era in which Allah responds, one bolstering the other. And they will contend against it in this world?!"

Abu Talib died three years before the Hijra. During that time, the Prophet began to hear more harm from his people; he saw them holding back from accepting his message, keeping the Arabs away from it, and repelling them from following him.

When Allah willed to strengthen His religion and fulfill His promise, the Messenger of Allah would go out during some of the pilgrimage seasons and present himself to the Arab tribes, reciting to them the signs of his Lord, as he had done every season. While he was at al-Aqaba, he encountered a group from al-Khazraj, for whom Allah intended good. He said to them: "Who are you?" They said: "From the Khazraj." He said: "The allies of the Jews?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you not sit with me so we may speak?" They said: "Yes."

They sat with him and he called them to Allah Almighty and presented Islam to them, reciting the Quran. There were Jews nearby, and they had told the Ansar that a prophet was about to arise at that time. When the Messenger of Allah spoke to these people and called them to Allah, they said to one another: "This is the very prophet those Jews told us of. Let us not allow the Jews to reach him before us."

They believed in the Prophet and in Allah his Lord, then departed — the Messenger of Allah bidding them farewell — and returned to their land, where they brought others to belief.

They were six men from the Khazraj:

From Banu al-Najjar — who is the Tayyim of Allah — then from Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar ibn Tha'labah ibn 'Amr ibn al-Khazraj ibn Haritha ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amir: As'ad ibn Zurara ibn Adas ibn 'Ubayd ibn Tha'labah ibn Ghannam ibn Malik ibn al-Nahar, known as Abu Umama.

And 'Awf ibn al-Harith ibn Rifa'ah ibn Sawad ibn Malik ibn Ghannam ibn Malik ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar — he is the son of Afra'.

And from Banu Zurayq ibn 'Amir ibn Zurayq ibn 'Abd al-Haritha ibn Malik ibn Ghadab ibn Hashm ibn al-Khazraj: Rafi' ibn Malik ibn al-'Ajlan ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amir ibn Zurayq.

And from Banu Salamah ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ali ibn Sarda ibn Yazid ibn Jashim ibn al-Khazraj, then from Banu Sawad ibn Ghannam ibn Ka'b ibn Salamah: Qutbah ibn 'Amir ibn Hudaydah ibn 'Amr ibn Ghannam ibn Sawad.

And from Banu Haram ibn Ka'b ibn Ghannam ibn Ka'b ibn Salamah: 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir ibn Nabi ibn Zayd ibn Haram.

And from Banu 'Ubayd ibn 'Adi ibn Ghannam ibn Ka'b ibn Salamah: Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab ibn al-Nu'man ibn Sinan ibn 'Ubayd.

When they embraced Islam, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have left behind a people among whom there is no greater evil and enmity than that which exists between them. May Allah unite them through you; if Allah unites them around you, there is no man more honored than you."

When the following year came, during the pilgrimage season, twelve men came to the Messenger of Allah at al-'Aqaba and pledged their allegiance to him after believing in Allah and accepting him. That was the first pledge of allegiance — likened to the pledge of women — in which fighting was not mentioned.

They included:

From Banu al-Najjar, then from Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar: As'ad ibn Zurara, and 'Awf and Mu'adh — the sons of al-Harith ibn Rifa'ah.

The Islam of As'ad ibn Zurara and 'Awf ibn al-Harith has already been mentioned.

And from Banu Zurayq ibn 'Amir: Rafi' ibn Malik ibn al-'Ajlan ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amir ibn Zurayq.

Dhakwan ibn 'Abd Qays ibn Khaldah ibn Mukhlad ibn 'Amir ibn Zurayq.

And from Banu 'Awf ibn al-Khazraj: 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit ibn Qays ibn Asram ibn Fahr ibn Tha'labah ibn Ghannam.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, who is Yazid ibn Tha'labah ibn Khazmah ibn Asram ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amara, from Banu Ghusayna, from Bali, as their ally.

And from Banu Salim ibn 'Awf ibn 'Amr ibn al-Khazraj, then from Banu al-'Ajlan ibn Zayd ibn Ghannam ibn Salim: al-'Abbas ibn 'Ubadah ibn Nadlah ibn Malik ibn al-'Ajlan.

And from Banu Salamah ibn 'Ali ibn Asad ibn Sarda ibn Yazid ibn Jashim ibn al-Khazraj, then from Banu Haram ibn Ka'b ibn Ghannam ibn Salamah: 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir ibn Nabi — his particulars have already been given.

And from Banu Sawad ibn Ghannam ibn Ka'b ibn Salamah: Qutbah ibn 'Amir ibn Hudaydah ibn 'Amr ibn Ghannam ibn Sawad.

Their embrace of Islam has already been mentioned.

And from al-Aws ibn Haritha ibn Tha'labah, then from Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal ibn Jashim ibn al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj: Abu al-Haytham ibn al-Tayhan, whose name is Malik.

And from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf ibn Malik ibn al-Aws: 'Uwaym ibn Sa'idah.

When the delegation departed from the Messenger of Allah, he sent with them Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr ibn Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf ibn 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusai. He instructed him to recite the Quran to them, to teach them Islam, and to instruct them in the religion. He thus became the first to be called one of the "reciters" in Medina. He would lead the Ansar in prayer, call them to Allah and His Messenger, and it was through his hands that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr came to Islam — and through them, all of Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal. After their conversion, not a single man or woman remained in the household of Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal except as a Muslim.

Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr then returned to Mecca, and the Ansar who had become Muslim set out for the pilgrimage season along with the polytheists of their people. The Messenger of Allah appointed a meeting with them at al-'Aqaba during the middle of the days of Tashreeq, for he desired his dignity, the victory of his Prophet, the honor of Islam and its people, and the humiliation of shirk and its people.

With the Messenger of Allah were 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, his uncle Hamza, and al-'Abbas — the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib. Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib said to the gathering: "O assembly of the Khazraj, Muhammad is from us, as you well know, and we have protected him from our people. He lives in honor among his people and in security in his land. He has, however, resolved to join you and attach himself to you. If you are prepared to be faithful to what you promise and to stand firm against those who oppose him, then so be it — but if you think you may abandon him and surrender him after he has come to you, then leave him now, for he is in a position of strength and protection among his people and his country."

The Ansar replied: "We have heard what you said. Speak now, O Messenger of Allah, and take for yourself what you wish."

The Messenger of Allah spoke, recited the Quran, and called to Allah; then he said: "I take your pledge on the condition that you protect me from what you protect your women and children." Al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur — one of the masters of the Ansar — took his hand and said: "Yes, by the One who sent you with the truth — we will protect you from all that we protect ourselves from. So take our pledge, O Messenger of Allah. By God, we are the sons of war and the people of the shield; we have inherited that from one generation to the next."

They then pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah at al-'Aqaba on the terms of Islam: that they would protect him as they protected their women and children, and that they would stand firmly by him.

The Messenger of Allah appointed twelve chieftains from among them. They were: As'ad ibn Zurara, 'Abdullah ibn Rawaha, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', Rafi' ibn Malik, al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, Usayd ibn Hudayr, Sa'd ibn Khayithama, and Abu al-Haytham ibn al-Tayhan.

He said to the chieftains: "You are the guarantors over your people — as the disciples of 'Isa ibn Maryam were guarantors for him — and I am the guarantor for those among my own people who have believed in me." They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." Then they set out for the city.

Ka'b ibn Malik recited the following, remembering them and addressing the polytheists of Quraysh:

> *Tomorrow has come upon the people and is now a reality —*
> *he told my father that good sense had slipped away from him.*
> *Keeping watch over the affairs of the people, alert and attentive —*
> *O God, do not let yourself be destroyed;*
> *with Ahmad, a light from Allah's guidance shines forth.*
> *He told Abu Sufyan that he had appeared before us —*
> *you cannot crowd out something that has taken its place.*
> *Gather whatever force you are able to gather.*
> *Father, you will prove a fool if you pursue this path,*
> *know well that we have broken our covenants with you.*
>
> *For your nose, if you dare attempt that brave act —*
> *its venom seeps in without a remedy.*
> *As for Ibn Rawaha — he will not yield it to him,*
> *but will honor it and raise its standing,*
> *with a Muslim who neither covets nor is greedy.*
> *And what of Ibn al-Rabi' when you deal with his covenant?*
> *He strives to fulfill what he has bound himself to —*
> *meeting every pledge he has given.*
> *Abu al-Haytham also fulfilled his pledge in full —*
> *are you so foolish as to think of nullifying this dispute?*
> *And what of Ibn Hudayr when you come against him —*
> *wounds, when I tested him, did not weigh on me.*
> *And Sa'd, the brother of 'Amr ibn 'Awf, is*
> *one upon whom the night closes in around you.*
> *Your foremost ones — do not tire yourself of them.*
> *His father al-Bara' and Ibn 'Amr, both of them —*
> *Awsad, his father al-Sa'di, and al-Mundhir —*
> *fulfillment personified — and al-Qawqali ibn Samit.*

edits.chapter_key: sermons, brotherhood, and the new community
edits.body_md:
The first sermon delivered by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was at the first Friday prayer gathered in Madinah. As Ibn Hisham narrated, he praised Allah and extolled Him as He deserves, then said:

"As for what follows — O people, send forth provision for yourselves. By Allah, one of you will surely be struck unconscious with no shepherd and no interpreter and no intercessor between him and his Lord. Then his Lord will say to him: 'Did My Messenger not come to you and convey the message? I gave you wealth and favored you — what have you put forward for yourself?' He will look to his right and see nothing, then to his left and see nothing, then before him and see nothing but the Fire. Whoever can shield his face from the Fire, even with half a date, let him do so. And whoever cannot find even that, let him do so with a good word, for a good deed is rewarded ten times over — up to seven hundred times over. And peace be upon you, and the mercy and blessings of Allah."

He, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, then delivered another sermon, in which he said:
