He ordered them to prepare and make ready, and he said: "O Allah, take from the eyes and news of the Quraysh and those with them, until they proclaimed it in their own country." So the people were prepared.

Hassan ibn Thabit spoke up, inciting the people and recalling the wounded men of Khuza'ah:

> *I have not seen the men of Bani Ka'b in the presence of Mecca,*
> *in the hands of men who did not draw their swords,*
> *and many people did not wear their armour.*
> *If only my hair could win you my victory?*
> *Suhail ibn 'Umar and her punishment —*
> *this is the time of war; he drew out its sinews.*
> *And Safwan — we long for the edge of his blade.*
> *If it is purely milked and I shave its fangs,*
> *then do not trust us, son of Umm Mahalid.*
> *She has a fall in death that opens her door,*
> *and do not fear us — for our swords are ready.*

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, assembled his forces to march on Mecca, Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah wrote a letter to the Quraysh informing them of what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, had resolved to do — namely, to march against them. He entrusted the letter to a woman — said to be a freed slave of some of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib — on the condition that she deliver it to the Quraysh. She concealed it in her hair, twisting her locks around it, and set out.

Then news of what Hatib had done came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, from heaven. He sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, saying: "Go — you will find a woman who has with her a letter that Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah wrote to the Quraysh, warning them of what we are gathering against them."

They set out and overtook her at a place known as the grove of Bani Abi Ahmad. They dismounted her from her mount, searched her baggage, and found nothing. Then 'Ali, peace be upon him, said to her: "By Allah, I have not lied and I have not been misled — bring out this letter, or we will strip your clothing." When she saw the resolve in him, she said, "I will show it." She turned away, loosened her braids, and drew out the letter from within them. She handed it over, and it was brought to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family.

He summoned Hatib and said, "What drove you to do this?"

Hatib said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am a believer in Allah and His Messenger — I have not changed nor wavered. But I was a man among the Quraysh who had no family or clan to protect his people and children there, so I sought to earn their favour through this."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O Messenger of Allah, let me strike his neck — he has committed treason." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "And what do you know, O 'Umar? Perhaps Allah has already looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you.'"

Then Allah revealed concerning Hatib: "O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, offering them affection, when they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, driving out the Messenger and yourselves because you believe in Allah, your Lord — if you have gone forth to strive in My cause and to seek My pleasure. You confide to them affection, while I know best what you have concealed and what you have revealed" — up to the words of the Almighty: "You have had a good example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people: 'We are innocent of you and of what you worship besides Allah. We disbelieve in you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever, until you believe in Allah alone.'" (al-Mumtahanah: 1–4)

And so on to the end of the passage.

Then the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, set out to conquer Mecca when ten nights of Ramadan had passed.

edits.chapter_key: ambush in the valley of hunayn
edits.body_md:
When the Hawazin tribes heard what had happened to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, and what Allah had granted him in the conquest of Makkah, Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri rallied them. He gathered together the Hawazin, all of Thaqif, all of Nasr and Jushm, Sa'd ibn Bakr, and a few from Banu Hilal. Of all the clans of Qays 'Aylan, only these few took part; the rest were absent. The Hawazin brought with them Ka'b and Kilab, though none of those clans distinguished themselves by name. Among Banu Jushm was a great elder, Duraid ibn al-Sammah, a man whose only remaining value was his judgment and experience in warfare; he was carried in a litter. Among Banu Thaqif there were Qarib ibn al-Aswad ibn Mas'ud ibn Mu'athib, and among Banu Malik there were Dhu al-Khimar Subay' ibn al-Harith ibn Malik and his brother Ahmar ibn al-Harith. Overall command of the people fell to Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri.

When Malik resolved to march against the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, he led the people out along with their wealth, their wives, and their children. When he descended upon Awtas, the people gathered around him, including Duraid ibn al-Sammah, who was carried in his litter to that place. Duraid asked: "In what valley are you camped?" They said: "In Awtas." He said: "Good terrain for horses — neither rocky enough to injure hooves nor so soft as to swallow them. But what is this I do not hear? No lowing of camels, no braying of donkeys, no crying of children, no wailing of women?" They told him: Malik ibn 'Awf had led the people out with their wealth, their wives, and their children.

He said: "Bring him to me." When Malik came before him, Duraid said: "O Malik, you have become the leader of your people, and this day will have days after it. Why do I hear no lowing of camels, no braying of donkeys, no crying of children, no wailing of women?" Malik replied: "I brought the people along with their wealth, their children, and their wives." Duraid said: "And why is that?" Malik said: "I wanted every man to feel that his family and his wealth were behind him, so that he would fight to defend them."

Duraid said: "By God, you think like a shepherd of sheep! Does a routed man ever save anything? In the end, nothing helps a man but his own sword and spear. If the battle goes against you, you will have exposed your family and your wealth."

Then he asked: "And what of the Kilab and Ka'b — did they witness this gathering?" They said: "None of them came." He said: "The men of resolve and seriousness were absent. Had this been the day of al-'Ala' and Rifa'a, neither Kilab nor Ka'b would have stayed away. Who from Amir's people is with you?" They said: "'Amr ibn 'Amir and 'Awf ibn 'Amir." He said: "Those two branches of Amir will neither help nor harm. O Malik, you have accomplished nothing by bringing the women and wealth before the horses — by 'egg' he meant property and women. Send them back to the highlands and put the fighting men on horseback. If you win, what lies behind you is yours; if you lose, at least you have preserved your family and your wealth."

Malik said: "By God, I will not do that. You have grown old and your mind has weakened with your age."

"Obey me, O assembly of Hawazin!" Malik called out. "Or I will fall upon this sword until it comes out through my back."

They disliked that Duraid ibn al-Sammah should have any say or influence in the matter, and so they said: "We obey you."

Duraid ibn al-Sammah said: "This is a day I have not witnessed before, and it has not stirred wonder in me." He said:

> *I wish it had a trunk*
> *I would hide within it*
> *I would lead and extinguish the impulse*
> *It is like a crack*

Then Malik said to the people: "When you see them, break off the hilts of your swords, then charge them as one man."

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was preparing to march against Hawazin, he was reminded that Safwan ibn Umayyah possessed shields and weapons. He sent a messenger to Safwan ibn Umayyah, who was at that time still a polytheist. He said to him: "O Safwan, lend us what you have of weapons so that we may meet our enemy tomorrow."

Safwan said: "O Muhammad, is this by compulsion?" The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "It is a guaranteed loan, to be returned to you in full." Safwan said: "In that case, there is no objection." It is said that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, borrowed from him a hundred shields, along with the weapons and equipment to carry them.

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, received word of Malik ibn 'Awf's movements, he departed Makkah on the twelfth — with ten thousand men, plus two thousand from the people of Makkah and ten thousand of his companions who had marched with him to the conquest of Makkah.

As the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, marched with the Muslims, 'Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami said:

> *From me, a letter of counsel, plainly set forth —*
> *carry it to Hawazin, to great and small alike.*
> *His army fills the breadth of earth, its farthest corners:*
> *I say the Messenger of God shall meet you in the morning.*
> *And the Muslims are the garment of God — Ghassan among them —*
> *in them I shield you whole, yet you have turned away.*
> *And the Ajraban: Banu 'Abs and Dhubyan are with him,*
> *and on his right, the support of Banu Asad,*
> *in their vanguard, Aws and 'Uthman.*
> *The earth near trembled beneath his awe.*

When the Muslims reached a place called Dhat Anwat — a tree — it was a tree the Quraysh had venerated in the time of ignorance. They would come to it every year, hang their weapons upon it, and slaughter animals beside it, staying near it for a day. Some of those who had recently embraced Islam called out to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "O Messenger of Allah, make for us a Dhat Anwat as they have one."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah is greater! By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you have said what the people of Moses said to Moses: 'Make for us a god as they have gods. He said: You are a people who are ignorant.'" (al-A'raf: 138) "It is the same pattern — you would follow the ways of those who came before you."

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, descended into the valley of Hunayn, he moved through a wide, hollow valley of the Tihama region in the darkness before dawn. The Hawazin and those who had joined them had arrived before him and lay in ambush in the ravines, bends, and narrow passages of the valley. They had gathered, drawn up their ranks, and made ready. The Muslims, advancing through that valley in loose order, were suddenly overwhelmed and broke into flight as one man; the men turned and retreated, and no one could be blamed.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, turned to the right and called out: "Come to me! Where are you going? I am the Messenger of Allah. I am Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah."

The people fled in defeat. Some of the hypocrites revealed what lay in their hearts. Abu Sufyan said: "This is a rout that will not be stopped until it reaches the sea." And another cried aloud: "Is not the magic defeated today?"

Five men of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib stood firm with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, sword in hand, shielding and striking for him; al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, who held the bridle of the Messenger of Allah's mule — and the Prophet was riding his white mule — Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, al-Fadl ibn al-'Abbas, and al-'Abbas himself.

It was also said that Qatham was not among them, but rather Ja'far ibn Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said to al-'Abbas — who was a man with a powerful voice — "Call to the people and let them know where I am."

The people had been routed, as Allah the Almighty has described in His words: "Indeed, Allah has given you victory on many fields — and on the day of Hunayn, when your great numbers pleased you but availed you nothing, and the earth, vast as it is, seemed to close in upon you; then you turned back in flight. Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers." (al-Tawbah: 25–26) — meaning those who remained steadfast with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, when the people fled.

Shayba ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Talha had resolved to kill the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. He said: "Today I shall avenge my father." His father had been killed on the day of Uhud. He said: "I drew close to the Messenger of Allah, but my heart was overwhelmed — it was as though something closed over me and held me back."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib looked and saw the man carrying the polytheists' standard — mounted on a camel, banner in hand — driving into the Muslims and pressing them hard as they fell back before Hawazin, with the enemy behind him. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, charged him, struck the camel's leg with his sword, felled the beast, and split the man's head open. The fallen camel became a barrier between the Muslims and the polytheists.

Al-'Abbas called out at the top of his voice: "O assembly of Muslims! O assembly of the Muhajirun! O assembly of the Ansar! O people of the Tree! O people of the Pledge of al-Ridwan — come to your Prophet!"

From every direction came the reply: "Labbaik! Labbaik!" Those who had fled were already beginning to realize that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, had not been killed and had not abandoned those who had turned back. Each man who wished to wheel his horse or camel around found he could not do so in the press and crush of the crowd, so he would take his weapons, cast himself from his mount, and make his way on foot to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his family.

When the polytheist standard-bearer was struck down, the enemy could no longer hold their position.

edits.chapter_key: awtas, ta'if, and the siege that failed
edits.body_md:
Their formation collapsed, their order dissolved, and their affairs fell into disarray. Allah Almighty struck them in their faces and supported His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, with a humiliation of the enemy the like of which had not been seen before, just as He has described in His Book. The last of those who had fled did not return until the captives were already sitting in the hands of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, and the spoils had been collected and were present.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, had on that day of tribulation a role that no one else matched. When the Ansar returned to the Messenger of Allah they stood well; and the Muhajirun were patient. The Messenger of Allah oversaw the men from his mount, watching as they fought, and said: "Now the furnace burns hot."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, turned to Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib during the rout, while he was holding the Prophet's mule, and asked: "Who is this?" He said: "I am your cousin, O Messenger of Allah." And he held firm at that hour, and his Islam proved good when he had embraced it.

He saw Umm Sulaym bint Milhan. She was with her husband Abu Talha, standing firm in the midst of the battle. She was pregnant with 'Abdullah ibn Abi Talhah, and Abu Talha's mount was with her. She was afraid the camel might throw her off, so she gripped its head, plunged her hand into the halter near the stern, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, spoke to her: She said: "Yes, by my father and mother, O Messenger of Allah — kill those who flee from you, as you kill those who fight you, for they deserve it."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "O mother, Allah is sufficient." It is said she had a dagger with her. Abu Talha asked her: "What is that dagger for, O Umm Sulaym?" She said: "I took it so that if any polytheist came near me, I would plunge it into him." Abu Talha then said: "Do you not hear, O Messenger of Allah, what Umm Sulaym al-Rumaysa' is saying?" — "Rumaysa'" referring to dirt that collects in the corner of the eye.

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was advancing toward Hunayn, Banu Sulaym joined him under al-Dahhak ibn Sufyan al-Kilabi, and they were with him. When the people were routed, Malik ibn 'Awf said, struck by what had befallen him:

> *The oldest proof is that this was a day of denial —*
> *a man like me, a man like you: shield and shield.*
> *If the company loses one day, and the burden falls,*
> *then I drove back ranks upon ranks.*
> *Battalions in full sight of eye —*
> *I may yet drive the thrust to its resounding mark.*
> *When the poor outlast the prosperous,*
> *and the nobles howl and flee from the thrust of the spear,*
> *a falling machine gun sweeps from the flanks,*
> *Tarat screams while we erupt forward,*
> *and the fox working within it is broken.*
> *O Zayd, son of their concern — where do you flee?*
> *The tooth has worn down and the age has grown long;*
> *the white banners have yielded to the long red lances.*
> *I have known nothing like her except immersion,*
> *when the Guards emerge from beneath the shadow.*

Abu Qatadah al-Ansari said: On the day of Hunayn, I saw two men fighting — one a Muslim and the other a polytheist — and a man from among the polytheists was trying to get his polytheist companion the upper hand over the Muslim. So I went at him, struck his hand, and cut it off. He then seized me with his other hand and held me so tightly that I feared he would kill me, but the bleeding weakened him until he fell, and I struck him and killed him.

When Allah defeated the polytheists and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was able to —

> *I swear by God, the plant deserves it —*
> *I have been absent from God's horses, the horses of Allat.*

When Hawazin was defeated, Thaqif suffered losses at Banu Malik, with seventy men killed under their banner, among them 'Uthman ibn 'Abd-Allah ibn Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith ibn Habib. Their banner had been carried by Dhu al-Khimar, and when he was killed, 'Uthman ibn 'Abd-Allah took it up and fought under it until he too was killed. When he fell, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "May God keep him away — he hated the Quraysh."

One of the Muslim women remarked on this.

The banner of the allied forces was held by the boat of Ibn al-Aswad. When the people were routed, he propped it against a tree, and then he, his cousins, and his kinsmen fled from the alliance. Of the allied forces, only two men were killed: a man from Jealousy, known as Wahb, and another from Banu Kubbah, known as al-Jalah. When word reached the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, that al-Jalah had been killed, he said: "Today the master of the youth of Thaqif was killed, except for the son of Hneida" — meaning Ibn Hunaida, al-Harith ibn Uwais.

When the polytheists were routed, they fell back to al-Ta'if with Malik ibn Auf. Some fled in haste while others headed toward a valley; those who made for the valley were none but Banu Jalah of Thaqif. The cavalry of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, pursued them. He pressed through the palm groves among the people and did not follow the well-worn path of the passes.

Rabi'ah ibn Rafi' al-Sulami caught up with Duraid ibn al-Samma, taking hold of the halter of his camel. He mistook Duraid for a woman, since Duraid was riding in a litter, and Rabi'ah intended to take him captive. But the man was an aged elder, and Rabi'ah did not recognize him.

Duraid said to him, "What do you want, young man?" He replied, "I will kill you." Duraid said, "And who are you?" He said, "I am Rabi'ah ibn Rafi' al-Sulami." He struck him with his sword, but it did nothing. Duraid told him, "Your mother has given you a poor weapon! Take that sword from behind the litter, strike with it, raise it above the bones, and bring it down on the brain — for that is how I used to strike men. But if you have lost your wits, then go back to your mother and tell her you have killed Duraid ibn al-Samma, and there will come a day when you will have kept your women from harm."

When Duraid fell and was exposed, his thighs were like parchment from a lifetime in the saddle.

When Rabi'ah returned to his mother and told her he had killed Duraid, she said, "By Allah, he freed three of your mothers."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, sent, in pursuit of those who had fled toward Awtaas, Abu 'Amir al-Ash'ari. He caught up with some of the defeated fighters and they battled him. Abu Amir was struck by an arrow and killed. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari then took up the banner and fought them, and they feared he would kill the Banu Nasr from Banu Riab.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, passed by a woman who had been killed by Khalid ibn al-Walid, and a crowd had gathered around her. He said, "Who killed this?" They said: Khalid ibn al-Walid. He sent word to Khalid through one of those with him, saying: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, forbids the killing of a child, a woman, or a hired laborer." And "al-Asif" means the hired man.

Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam fought fiercely that day. Malik ibn 'Awf positioned himself and those with him at a mountain pass to cover the retreat of their vulnerable so that they might get away safely.

The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said regarding Bajad: "If you are able to find him, do not let him escape you." Bajad was a man from Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr. The Muslims captured him along with his family, and with them was al-Shayma' bint al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-'Ari, the foster sister of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family. Those who captured her treated her roughly during the march, but she said: "I am your companion's foster sister." They did not believe her, and when she was brought before the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, she said: "I am your sister from breastfeeding." He said: "And what is the sign of that?" She said: "A bite you gave me on my back when I was carrying you."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, spread out his robe for her, seated her upon it, and treated her with kindness, and said: "If you wish, you may stay with me in honor and love, and I shall hold you dear, or if you wish, I will provide for you and return you to your people." She said: "Rather, provide for me and return me to my people." And she chose that. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, returned her to her people.

From the Quraysh: Ayman ibn Ubayd. Yazid ibn Zama'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza — he had a mare called "The Wing," and he was killed by her.

From the Ansar: Saraqa ibn al-Harith ibn 'Adi, from Banu al-'Ajlan.

From the Ash'aris: Abu 'Amir al-Ash'ari.

The captives of Hunayn were brought together before the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. He ordered that the captives and the spoils be held at al-Ji'ranah, and they were kept there.

Al-'Abbas ibn Mardas al-Sulami spoke verses recalling the boat of Ibn al-Aswad and his flight on the day of Hunayn, and al-Khimar — and the imprisonment of his people that led to their ruin:

> *Except for the measure of Ghaylan from me, for I am the one with knowledge.*
> *And a saying other than what you say is plausible,*
> *and a reply — yet I give an answer.*
> *By God, who neither strays nor leads astray,*
> *Muhammad is the slave and the Messenger.*
> *Every youth calls on him for good,*
> *we found him a prophet like Moses.*
> *Glory when things are apportioned,*
> *and the matter is made clear by the command of Banu Fassi.*
> *A prince, and the circles may turn —*
> *they lost their standing, and to every people*
> *the soldiers of God are a suburb on the march.*
> *So we found for them a lion of the forest.*
> *We were right — we almost took flight —*
> *the gathering of Banu Fassi, the gathering of Banu Fassi.*
> *They were joined by soldiers and did not hold their ground.*
> *I swear, if they had not been killed before us,*
> *we would have embraced it, and the victories were handed over.*
> *So why were we lions — and then made even?*
> *He rode off, and the blood in it was like dates,*
> *and the day before I had that longing.*
> *No male people have heard the like of it —*
> *you have not heard of it for a day.*
> *On its banners the horses were forged;*
> *we said in the dust: Banu Hitit —*
> *they have a mind that punishes, or cunning.*
> *And Dhu al-Khimar was no leader of a people;*
> *things became plain to whoever beheld them.*
> *He drove them according to the way of the Munaya,*
> *and many of them were slain.*
> *So I said: those who survived among them were wounded,*
> *or shut within the narrow confines, creaking.*
> *It does not befit matters to be kin to delay —*
> *they held sway and ruled their affairs, and the falcons escaped.*
> *I revile her — the peacocks and the barley —*
> *and Abu Auf stands apart from them.*
> *I divided the houses and palaces:*
> *if it were not for the boat and its sons,*
> *on Yemen, referred to by the Field Marshal,*
> *but the presidency spread wide,*
> *and dreams of glory grew,*
> *they obeyed a settled chieftain though they had grandfathers —*
> *the noses of the people were not tanned by the samir.*
> *In God's war they have no supporter;*
> *the Banu Ghazia fled in every direction.*
> *As the Banu Sa'd ruled and turned,*
> *to Islam is a deception —*
> *it is as though Banu Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr*
> *had been absolved of the tenderness of the breast.*
> *Awaken us — surrender, I am your protector —*
> *from some after the ladder.*
> *It is as though the people, when they came to us,*
> *if they embrace Islam, they will turn away,*
> *and if they do not surrender, the call to prayer is made.*

Al-'Abbas ibn Mardas al-Sulami also spoke on the day of Hunayn:

> *So I see you — the workshops have been dissolved.*
> *Pardon a man from his family, and he is glad.*
> *Rest, and spend the time at the neighborhood mosque —*
> *a house of no — O lamb — for most of our lives.*
> *Milk, the past of a living sustenance returning,*
> *a grain touched by the alienation of the kernels.*
> *If you seek the unbelievers, you are not to blame.*
> *I am a minister of the Prophet, and he continued —*
> *bundle and the bitterness of them, and wide.*
> *We summoned the finest delegation to them,*
> *a gift for them of the weave of David — wondrous.*
> *So we are with a thousand of Sulaym upon them;*
> *the hand of God between the two woods is pledged —*
> *pledged to the beloved, yet*
> *with our swords and bright, fallen caps.*
> *So well done, O Mahdi — Mecca taken by force,*
> *intimate and now soaked in the blood of the unbelievers.*
> *Openly, and the horses are yielding their bodies to us,*
> *narrowed with the broken souls.*
> *And a day of longing when Hawazin came —*
> *the striking of the enemies among them, and the realities.*
> *Our patience with laughter does not weary us;*
> *a brilliant cloud, a thunderous brigade,*
> *before the Messenger of God, who towers above us,*
> *with the sword of the Messenger of God — and death is like it —*
> *on the eve of the laugh of Ibn Sufyan Mu'attab.*
> *We were the closest to following.*
> *Defend us from our brother, even if we see —*
> *we accepted it with guidance and laws.*
> *But the religion of God is the religion of Muhammad,*
> *and God's command has no hindrance.*
> *He abided in it after the prayer and commanded us.*

Buhayr ibn Zuhayr ibn Abi Salma said on the day of Hunayn:

> *When terror diminished every coward —*
> *the lad is God's, and His slave, and orphaned —*
> *on the day of love for our peers,*
> *and swimmers pouring forth to the ears,*
> *and distilled with your fingers and gum,*
> *from the shape of his garment in his palm.*
> *And He honored us through worship of the Most Merciful.*
> *God honored us and made our religion plain,*
> *and humiliated them through worship of Satan.*
> *I swear by God, He destroyed them and scattered their gathering.*

Ibn Hisham said: Some narrators reported the following: When the uncle of your Prophet and his guardian stood and called: "O battalion of faith! Where are those who answered their God on the day of al-Ara'id and al-Ridwan?"

Malik ibn 'Awf said, excusing his flight:

> *Yes, along the stretches of the road,*
> *preventing sleep — I do not close an eye for an hour.*
> *Did Hawazin harm its enemy?*
> *And the eyes of one who loves her — if he is penalized —*
> *two of them are Hasif and Blame,*
> *and a battalion I clothed in armor.*
> *I presented it, and the witnesses of the nation know better,*
> *and the forerunner of the affliction of souls at his distress —*
> *they want to flood him and drown him in blood.*
> *I forgave him and left our brothers to his account.*
> *The glory of life — and no sheep is divided.*
> *If his floods recede, he will reveal himself to me,*
> *and God knows best who held back and who wronged.*
> *You cost me the destruction of the family of Muhammad,*
> *and you abandoned me as you fight,*
> *and you abandoned me when I fight — alone.*
> *One and another are not equal.*
> *In the world he grows for the highest,*
> *and the winter hastens.*
> *Sahma was presented with the spear of Saljam —*
> *I despised it as a machine of fornication.*
> *And she says: not so-and-so,*
> *and I let his place reply — and why?*
> *Like the durry — impossible and shameful —*
> *and I braced myself for the weight of the spears.*

It is said regarding Hawazin that they also recounted their journey to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family — with Malik ibn Auf after his embrace of Islam:

> *And your wealth above them — the banners fluttering —*
> *I remember their path to the people when they gathered.*
> *A day of longing — the crown shines,*
> *and Malik, Malik — none surpassed him.*
> *They had strength, bodies, and resolve.*
> *Until they met hardship when hardship met them —*
> *before the Prophet, until the dusk of paradise.*
> *So they scattered the people until none could be seen;*
> *from the heavens — defeated and embraced.*
> *Then Jibril descended with their victory.*
> *From us — and even if it were not Jibril fighting beside us —*
> *for our delight, our swords are liberation.*
> *With a thrust, or even the saddle of leeches,*
> *'Umar al-Faruq saw them broken and defeated.*

Then came the Battle of Ta'if:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, marched to Ta'if after returning from Hunayn. Thaqif, upon the arrival of the Prophet at Ta'if, shut the city gates against him and prepared their fortifications for battle.

Ka'b ibn Malik composed the following verses when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, assembled his forces for the march to Ta'if:

> *We have swept all doubt from Tihamah,*
> *and from Khaybar — then we drew our swords.*
> *Choose your course; and if she were to speak,*
> *she would say: step forward, or thrust.*
> *In the courtyard of your house stand thousands of us,*
> *making your home a place of departure.*
> *Thrones are seized with courage and resolve,*
> *and swift horses come to you.*
> *Leaving behind a multitude in their wake,*
> *she has what I have made her feel assured of.*
> *The terminologists ring out with the hatufa;*
> *India's fortunes did not strike Kativa.*
> *Like the truths I have preserved as proverbs —*
> *the day after the relief of Jad'a Medua.*
> *I am no nurse if you do not see it:*
> *when they descend into your space, you will hear —*
> *in their hands, delicate squirrels.*
> *Imagine the earnestness of heroes within it.*
> *And a resolve that was no light twist,*
> *wise and knowing, rightly guided.*
> *Among the nations, we had a corporal —*
> *do I find they have no counsel?*
> *He told them that we had assembled,*
> *mounted on horses, eager for battle,*
> *and I brought them crawling forward,*
> *surrounding the lined wall of their share.*
> *Pure of heart and fragrant in abstinence,*
> *their leader was Albi, who was crucified.*
> *He was shown mercy toward us.*
> *Obey us and obey God,*
> *and make yourself a support and a refuge for us.*
> *If they offer us peace, we will accept,*
> *and we show no weakness or trembling.*
> *But if you refuse, we will fight you with patience*
> *until you submit to Islam.*
> *We fight until we are slain or prophesy —*
> *did we hope for the thalad or the spectrum?*
> *We strive, caring not whom we encounter,*
> *the core of the afflicted among them and the ally.*
> *How many people turned away from us —*
> *so we braved ears and noses.*
> *They did not see them as capable,*
> *yet he drives them with force,*
> *with every supple, heavy Muhannad blade.*
> *The religion is moderate and true,*
> *the command of God and Islam supreme.*
> *And rob her of necklaces and adornments,*
> *and leave behind the exposure —*
> *and whoever does not abstain will face eclipse.*
> *So they accepted and were reassured.*

Shaddad ibn 'Arid al-Jashmi said in commemoration of the journey of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, to Ta'if:

> *How can he be aided who finds no victory,*
> *and did not fight alongside her stones in vain?*
> *They are not human beings from among her people —*
> *do not support al-Lat; God will destroy it.*
> *The one that burned in the dam caught fire —*
> *when will the Prophet come down to your land?*

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, marched along the Palm of Yemen, then along a pass, then along the salt flats, then across the sea of foam from Layyah, where he built a mosque — one that remains a seasonal landmark.

At that time, a man from Banu Layth who had killed a man from Hudhayl was brought before him — and this was the first blood case adjudicated in Islam.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, ordered the fortress of Malik ibn Auf to be demolished, and the march continued until the army descended near a Sidra tree. It is said that it was forbidden to approach the property of a man who was close to the wealth of a man of Thaqif, and so the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, sent word to him: either surrender, or we will tear down your wall. He refused to accept Islam, and so the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, ordered his wall to be destroyed.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, then advanced until he camped near Ta'if. He positioned his army there, and men accompanying him fell, because Thaqif's soldiers descended from the wall of Ta'if and shot arrows that reached them. When the fallen were among them, he moved his army to where his mosque in Ta'if stands today.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, besieged them for twenty nights — some say seventeen.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, had two of his wives with him. One of them, Umm Salamah, was sheltered between two tent poles, and he prayed between the two intervals. When Thaqif later embraced Islam, they built a mosque over the prayer site of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family — the mosque of 'Amr ibn Ummah ibn Wahb ibn Mu'tab ibn Malik.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, fought fierce battles against them throughout the days of the siege, and they found themselves worn down by it.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, ordered a catapult to be constructed and stones were hurled at the people of Ta'if. When the stones began to pile up and break through part of the wall, a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, crept beneath a protective tank and pushed it toward the wall of Ta'if in order to breach it. Thaqif responded by hurling upon them an iron beam wrapped in fire. The men scrambled out from beneath the tank, and Thaqif killed a number of them. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, then commanded — alongside his forces — that the grape vineyards of Thaqif be cut down, and the Muslims carried this out.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said, while the siege was still heavy upon him: "Permission has not been granted to conquer Ta'if." When this became known to the Muslims, they questioned him about it, and he confirmed it. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, then give the order to withdraw." And so the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the herald to call it out, and the call for withdrawal was made.

'Uyaynah ibn Husn al-Fazari said: Thaqif is a glorious and honorable people. Some Muslims said to him: "You praise the polytheists, yet you came to support the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family!" He replied: "I did not come to fight Thaqif alongside you. What I wanted was for Muhammad to open Ta'if, so that Thaqif might capture a slave girl, whom I would acquire, that she might bear me a son — for they are a people of noble stock."

While the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, were besieging Ta'if, some enslaved people came down to him, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, freed them.

Isma'il ibn Aban narrated, with his isnad, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari, who said:

"The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, withdrew into his chamber while he was besieging Ta'if, and he prolonged his private counsel with 'Ali, while the people looked on. Many envied me for what he had singled him out with. Allah and His Messenger" — until Abu Bakr and 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have prolonged since today your private counsel with 'Ali." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "It was not I who chose him — it was God who chose him."

All the people came to know the distinction that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his God had accorded to his guardian 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, drawing him close above all other Companions — such that none among them had been granted his favor during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah.

In the isnad of Abu Ghassan, from 'Ali, peace be upon him, he said:

"When Allah, exalted be He, revealed: 'O you who believe, when you consult the Messenger in private, offer charity before your consultation' (al-Mujadilah: 12) — 'Ali, peace be upon him, said: I possessed a dinar, which I exchanged for ten dirhams. Whenever I wished to consult the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, I would give a dirham in charity before doing so, until it was spent. No other Muslim did this. Then Allah, exalted be He, revealed: 'Are you fearful of having to give charity before your consultation? Then when you do not, and Allah has pardoned you' (al-Mujadilah: 12) — to the end of the verse. No one fulfilled the verse of al-Najwa other than me."

This is agreed upon among Muslims, and both al-Zamakhshari and al-Tha'labi mentioned in their commentary on this verse that no one among the Muslims acted upon the verse of al-Najwa except 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him.

His virtues are many and well-known, and those who deny his virtue, associated with it, have rejected most of them. Neither Abu Bakr, nor 'Umar, nor any other Companion is cited in connection with the verse of al-Najwa, nor is there any mention of them in it.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, placed his mouth to my ear and opened to me a thousand doors of knowledge, and from each of those doors a thousand more doors were opened to me.

None of the Companions received anything like this. Yet Abu Bakr said: "I am your guardian, and I am not the best among you." And among you is the one who is "he" whose horizon is mine.

'Umar said: "Do not exaggerate in the dowries of women — the most the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, ever gave to any of his wives was ten ounces."

A woman who was not among the most learned stood up and said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, have you not prevented us from a right that Allah has obligated for us? He said: 'And if you wish to take one wife in place of another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, take nothing from it'" (al-Nisa': 20) — to the end of the verse. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab felt ashamed and turned to those around him, saying: "You hear such a thing from me and do not object — until a woman who knows little corrects me?"

Many such instances could be cited had we not already exceeded what we set out to recount — but we have mentioned them here in connection with the private counsel of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, with his cousin, and his distinction above others. The denial of those who deny this amounts to a challenge to the Prophet, and they dare to prefer over him one who belongs to the people of preference.

Those who were martyred at Ta'if numbered twelve Muslims: seven from Quraysh, four from the Ansar, and one from Banu Layth.

After the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, departed from Ta'if following the fighting and siege, Bujayr ibn Zuhayr composed verses recalling Hunayn and Ta'if:

> *Tomorrow — Awtaas, and the day of lightning —*
> *it was a wound in the heart of Hunayn.*
> *Gathered by the seduction of Hawazin, they were gathered,*
> *then scattered like a torn bird.*
> *Except their wall and the belly of the trench —*
> *they did not hold us back from a single position.*
> *So they fortified themselves behind a closed door,*
> *and we were left to draw them out.*
> *You may divide leadership and meet —*
> *the screaming moved across the harass as though I*
> *see Hasran bounding back to Rahraja.*
> *Shahba' shines with the hopes of the Legion —*
> *we embraced a shadow as though it had never been created,*
> *green Lumma, when they hurl it.*
> *Like the prohibition — the smell of the taraq drifts —*
> *in every vanguard, should you fail to be caught.*
> *Hadal touches their longing, our sandals —*
> *from the weaving of David and the family of Muharraq.*

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, departed from Ta'if, and it was said to him: "Pray against Thaqif, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "O Allah, guide Thaqif and bring them to us."

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, reached al-Ji'ranah, the people of Hawazin came to him and asked him to return their wives and children. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, among the captives are your aunts, your maternal relations, and the women who nursed and raised you. Even if we were like al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr or al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, and he then came down to us with what he had received, we would beg for his generosity — and you are the best of those who are generous. We have come to you as Muslims."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Which is dearer to you — your wealth, or your women and children?"

They replied: "O Messenger of Allah, you have given us a choice between our wealth and our lineage. Our wives and our children are dearer to us."

Hawazin had been taken as captives — six thousand in all, comprising women, camels, and sheep beyond counting.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "As for what belongs to me and to the family of 'Abd al-Muttalib, it is yours. And when I lead the people in the Dhuhr prayer, stand and say: We are —" The people stood and said what he had commanded them. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whatever belonged to me and to the sons of Abd al-Muttalib is yours." The Muhajiroon and the Ansar said: "Whatever belonged to us is for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his family." Al-Aqra' ibn Habis said: "As for me and Banu Tamim, no." Uyaynah ibn Husn said: "As for me and Banu Fazarah, no." Abbas ibn Mardas said: "As for me and Banu Sulaym, no." But the Banu Sulaym said: "Yes — whatever was ours belongs to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his family." At that, Abbas ibn Mardas said to his own people of Banu Sulaym: "And you are content with this?"

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever holds fast to his share of these captives shall receive six shares from the first spoils I acquire as compensation." The people had no wives or children among the captives except Uyaynah ibn Husn, who had captured an old woman. He said: "I count her of noble lineage in her clan, and perhaps a great ransom will come for her." Abu Surad Zuhayr ibn Surad said to him: "Give her up — by Allah, her breast gives no milk, her belly bears no child, her husband is gone, and her youth is spent." So he returned her in exchange for six shares of compensation, once Zuhayr had said what he said. It is claimed that Uyaynah later regretted it.

Al-Aqra' ibn Habis complained to the Prophet about this and said: "By Allah, you have not given to a man of standing, nor to one of influence."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Tell Malik that if he comes to me as a Muslim, his family and his wealth will be returned to him, and I will give him a hundred camels." Malik did so and came out from Ta'if. He had feared that the people of Ta'if would learn of this and detain him, so he slipped away under cover of night. He then came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and met him at al-Ji'ranah or Makkah, and there he submitted to Islam. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, restored his family and his wealth to him and gave him a hundred camels.

Malik ibn Awf said, upon becoming Muslim:

> *Who among all people is like Muhammad?*
> *Never have I seen or heard of anyone like him.*
> *When you seek to know what tomorrow will bring,*
> *he delivers and gives to the lowly when imitated.*
> *With the polished spear he strikes every keen blade,*
> *and if scribes were to count their ranks,*
> *in the midst of confusion, he stands watch like a sentinel —*
> *as though he stands guard over his cubs.*

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, then appointed Malik over those of his people who had accepted Islam, from the surrounding tribes. These tribes had caused persistent trouble, and he fought them hard, never ceasing to raid them until they were subdued. Abu Muhajin ibn Habib ibn Amr ibn Umayr al-Thaqafi said:

> *Then Banu Salamah brought us comfort —*
> *the enemies press in on every side.*
> *They broke their covenant and violated what was sacred,*
> *yet I have no concern for them.*
> *We were the first to rebuke them,*
> *and still they came against our homes.*

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, finished returning the captives, he rode on. The people called out: "O Messenger of Allah, divide among us the spoils — the camels and the sheep!" They pressed him so urgently that his robe was pulled from him as he was backed against a tree. He said: "Return my robe to me, O people! By Allah, if you had as many camels as the trees of Tihamah, I would divide them all among you, and you would not find me miserly, cowardly, or a liar." He then went to a camel, took a tuft of hair from its hump, held it up between his fingers and said: "O people, by Allah, I have nothing of your spoils — not even this thread — that is not returned to you. So hand over even the needle and thread, for those who steal from the spoils will carry their shame before their families on the Day of Resurrection."

It is related that Aqeel ibn Abi Talib came home on the day of Hunayn to his wife Fatimah bint Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, his sword still stained with blood. She said: "I know you fought bravely — so what did you bring from the spoils of the polytheists?" He said: "I have nothing but this needle." Then he heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, proclaim that whoever had taken anything must return it, and that even a needle and thread must be given back. Aqeel said to his wife: "I think you have lost your needle." He then took it from her and went and threw it back into the spoils.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, gave generously to those whose hearts were to be won over — people who had submitted to Islam out of worldly desire and ambition. By winning them over with gifts, he hoped to draw them closer to Islam. He gave Abu Sufyan ibn Harb one hundred camels, and he gave his son Mu'awiyah one hundred camels as well. Hakim ibn Hizam received one hundred camels, and al-Harith ibn al-Harith ibn Kaldah's son received one hundred camels. A man from Banu Abd al-Dar also received one hundred camels; it was said he was Nusayr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaldah.

Al-Harith ibn Hisham received one hundred camels, Suhayl ibn Amr received one hundred camels, Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza received one hundred camels, and al-Ala ibn Jariyah al-Thaqafi — an ally of Banu Zahra — received one hundred camels. Uyaynah ibn Husn ibn Hudhayfah ibn Badr received one hundred camels, al-Aqra ibn Habis al-Tamimi received one hundred camels, Malik ibn Awf al-Nasri received one hundred camels, and Safwan ibn Umayyah received one hundred camels. Men from the Quraysh below that rank received less than one hundred.

Abbas ibn Mardas received less than a hundred camels and was aggrieved by this. He reproached the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him:

> *Early in the morning at al-Jarra,*
> *she was one who plundered three.*
> *If the people settle down, I shall not settle —*
> *my salvation is that the people sleep.*
> *Between Uyaynah and al-Aqra*
> *I have grown weary while my game was plundered.*
> *I was given nothing, nor was I withheld —*
> *yet I was present in the war that was turned aside,*
> *among its many raids.*
> *Except that she was given —*
> *they have surpassed my sheikh in the assembly,*
> *though he was neither a stronghold nor a prisoner.*
> *Whoever is diminished today will not rise again,*
> *and I was not without my place among them.*

The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Go to him and silence his tongue with gifts." So they gave him until he was satisfied.

It was said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "Al-Aqra ibn Habis was given one hundred camels, and Uyaynah ibn Husn was given one hundred camels, while Ja'il ibn Suraqah al-Damri was passed over." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, Ja'il ibn Suraqah is better than the whole earth filled with the likes of Uyaynah ibn Husn and al-Aqra ibn Habis. But I gave to those two in order to draw them toward surrender, while I entrusted Ja'il ibn Suraqah to his Islam."

Dhu al-Khuwaysirah — who was from Banu Tamim — came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, while he was distributing the spoils among the people, and said: "O Muhammad, you have not been just in what you have divided." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, grew angry and said: "Woe to you — if I am not just, then who is?"

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, then said: "From his followers will come a group who immerse themselves so deeply in religion that they pass right through it, just as an arrow passes clean through its target — nothing remains on the arrowhead, nothing on the shaft, nothing on the fletching. They will have gone beyond even the blood."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "They are the worst of creation, and the best of creation will be those who kill them." And those are the Khawarij who rose up against the Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and whom he killed at Nahrawan.

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, gave generously to those he gave — the Quraysh and the Arab tribes — while the Ansar received nothing, Hassan ibn Thabit composed verses reproaching this:

> *For the graceful women who neither bowed nor sacrificed,*
> *nor hastened for the sake of Allah and made their confession —*
> *if she is a lesson fashioned from pearls,*
> *full of grace, neither profane nor violated,*
> *and you find a smile within her smile,*
> *a glance and the worst of connections the visitor brings —*
> *leave Shama for you as her affection was*
> *for the faithful, if there are no others,*
> *when the prophet came and said: O finest of the trusted —*
> *they gave up their homes and gave victory.*
> *The banner is called Salim and May is uprooted —*
> *those who bear the guidance through the raging storm of war.*
> *Allah named them Helpers for their aid;*
> *the worries of the eye's corner slope inward —*
> *except for swords and the tips of the lances and a single button.*
> *And the people crowd around you for what is not ours,*
> *and do not let what the wall implies go to waste.*
> *We deliver people and keep no one back,*
> *and when its fire blazes, it is bought dearly —*
> *and do not let the makers of war call us*
> *the hope of the wakeful — among us the peg is driven home.*
> *As we turned back Badr without their entering it,*
> *if they fought their parties with a hero, it is of consequence.*
> *And we were your soldiers on the day of the throttle at Uhud —*
> *we stumbled, and all the people stumbled.*
> *So what did we say, and what did we imagine, and what were we told?*

The Ansar felt it keenly when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, distributed the spoils among others and left them with nothing, until many of them were saying: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, has found his own people."

So Sa'd ibn Ubadah al-Ansari went in to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, a number of the Ansar have taken it hard that you did not include them in what you divided among your people — the great gifts you bestowed on the tribes of the Arabs — while the Ansar received nothing of it."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: "And where do you stand in all of this, Sa'd?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am only a man of my people." The Prophet said: "Gather your people for me in this enclosure."

When they had gathered, Sa'd came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and said: "The Ansar have assembled." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, came to them, praised Allah and gave Him His due, then said: "O community of the Ansar, what is this talk that has reached me from you — this grievance you feel toward me? Did I not find you astray and Allah guided you? Were you not poor and Allah enriched you? Were you not enemies to one another and Allah made your hearts one?" They said: "Yes — to Allah and His Messenger belong grace and bounty." Then he said: "Will you not answer me, O community of the Ansar?" They said: "And what shall we say in answer to you, O Messenger of Allah? To Allah and His Messenger belong grace and credit." He said: "By Allah, if you wished, you could say — and you would be telling the truth, and you would be believed — 'You came to us rejected, we believed in you, we supported you, we struggled alongside you, and we brought you joy. You have appointed, O community of the Ansar, a portion of your kinship through which you have bound people to submit to you. I entrust you to your Islam. Are you not content that the people depart with worldly goods while you return with the Messenger of Allah? By Him in whose hand Muhammad's soul rests, had it not been for the Hijrah I would have been a man of the Ansar. If the people took one path and the Ansar took another, I would follow the path of the Ansar. O Allah, have mercy on the Ansar, the sons of the Ansar, and the sons of the sons of the Ansar.'"

The Ansar wept until their beards were wet, and they said: "We are content with the Messenger of Allah as our lot and our fortune." And they parted from him.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, departed from al-Ji'ranah to perform 'Umrah. He ordered the remainder of the fay' to be held at Majannah, in the region of Marr al-Zahran. When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, had completed his 'Umrah, he set out for Madinah and appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd as his deputy over Mecca. Mu'adh ibn Jabal was left with him to teach the people the Quran and instruct them in religion. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, provided them with the remainder of the fay'. His 'Umrah was in Dhu al-Qa'dah, and he arrived in Madinah during the nights of Dhu al-Qa'dah. That year he led the people on the pilgrimage — with 'Attab ibn Usayd.
